practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of a closed skill?
A) A football player receiving a through pass from a teammate
B) A gymnast performing a cartwheel on the floor exercise mat
C) A hockey player hitting a moving ball past a goalkeeper
D) A netball player intercepting a pass during a match
practice_questions.marks: B) A gymnast performing a cartwheel on the floor exercise mat [1 mark]. The environment is stable and predictable; the movement can be planned and repeated identically. All other options involve unpredictable, changing environments (open skills).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ability' in the context of sport and physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: ability is an innate / natural / inherited characteristic. 1 mark for development: it is stable and largely unchangeable; it underpins a performer's potential to learn and perform skills (accept: it sets a ceiling on what a performer can achieve). Do not credit definitions that describe ability as learned or practised.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a swimming coach could use the four skill classification continuums to analyse a performer's front crawl stroke.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for each continuum correctly applied with a brief justification (max 3 continuums credited). Examples: Basic/complex — complex, because it requires simultaneous coordination of arm pull, leg kick, breathing pattern and head position (1). Open/closed — closed, because the pool environment is stable and the performer moves through predictable conditions (1). Self-paced/externally paced — self-paced, because the swimmer decides their own stroke rate and turn timing (1). Gross/fine — gross, because large muscle groups of the arms, shoulders, core and legs produce the movement (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a basketball player taking a free throw is classified differently on the open/closed continuum compared to the same player making a lay-up during open play. Use the definitions of open and closed skills in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a free throw is a closed skill. 1 mark for justification: the environment is stable and predictable; the player stands at the same spot, no defenders can challenge, and the timing is self-controlled. 1 mark for identifying that a lay-up in open play is an open skill (or further towards the open end). 1 mark for justification: the environment is unpredictable; defenders are moving, teammates are repositioning, and the player must adapt their movement and timing to the changing situation.

practice_questions.text: A Year-10 PE teacher is designing classification tasks for two groups: one group will practise hitting a stationary ball on a tee, the other will practise hitting a ball bowled at them by a partner. Analyse how the four continuums differ between these two tasks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses all four continuums, clearly differentiating both tasks on each, with precise definitions and specific justifications rooted in the scenario. Points might include: basic/complex — hitting a stationary ball is more basic (fewer decisions, simpler movement), while hitting a bowled ball is more complex (timing judgement, footwork, range of shots possible); open/closed — stationary ball is closed (environment controlled, ball position fixed), bowled ball is open (ball direction, speed, bounce variable); self-paced/externally paced — tee hit is self-paced (performer starts when ready), bowled ball is externally paced (bowler dictates timing); gross/fine — both are gross skills (large muscle groups driving the shot) but the tee hit may be slightly more fine near the point of contact. Consistent reference to both tasks throughout.

Secure: Correctly analyses at least three continuums, with most justifications accurate. Generally applies to both tasks but may be less precise on one or two.

Developing: Names and partially explains two or three continuums. May label without justifying, or analyse only one task.

Emerging: Names one or two continuums; limited or no justification; may confuse continuum definitions.

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old club athlete competes in both archery and rugby union. Evaluate the view that classifying skills on the four continuums helps coaches plan training more effectively than simply labelling skills as 'easy' or 'hard'. Use examples from both sports in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, each applied to specific sporting examples from archery and/or rugby, with a clear and justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the four continuums reveal specific training needs — knowing an archery shot is closed, self-paced and fine tells a coach to prioritise consistency of technique and mental routine rather than reaction speed or physical power; classifying a rugby tackle as open, externally paced and gross directs training towards reactive drills and contact conditioning rather than technical precision; using continuums prevents coaches from applying the wrong training prescription, e.g. drilling a rugby player in closed-skill repetition when open-skill adaptability is what match performance demands; continuums allow comparison of a performer's current skill level to the demands of the full game situation. Arguments against or limitations: classifying skills is time-consuming and most coaches work intuitively from experience; the four continuums may oversimplify — many skills shift along continuums depending on context (a tennis serve is closed when initiating but the rally is open); beginners may benefit more from straightforward 'easy/hard' progression than from theoretical classification. Justified conclusion: the four continuums are most useful when planning training progression, especially when designing drills that match real competition demands.

Secure: Two or three points on each side, mostly applied to both sports, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development; sporting context present but thin or one-sport only.

Emerging: One-sided or very basic response; little or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Name the bone that sits in front of the knee joint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: patella / kneecap.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'blood cell production' as a function of the skeleton.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that red bone marrow produces blood cells; 1 mark for specifying red blood cells (which carry oxygen to working muscles) or white blood cells / platelets.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the skeleton in providing protection during sport. Give one example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that flat bones protect vital organs; 1 mark for an explanation (e.g. the ribs and sternum form a cage around the heart and lungs, or the cranium encases the brain); 1 mark for application to a named sporting context (e.g. the ribcage absorbs impact forces in a rugby tackle, protecting the heart and lungs from direct damage).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the design of the femur and its joint at the hip allows a wider range of movement than the joint at the knee.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the hip as a ball-and-socket joint; 1 mark for explaining that the rounded head of the femur fits into the cup-shaped socket of the pelvis, allowing movement in multiple directions (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, circumduction); 1 mark for correctly identifying the knee as a hinge joint; 1 mark for explaining that the shape of the joint restricts movement to one plane only (flexion and extension), which limits range but provides stability for weight-bearing activities.

practice_questions.text: A county-level hockey player relies on her skeleton for a range of functions during a match. Analyse how two functions of the skeleton contribute to her performance during the game.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two functions are clearly identified and developed with accurate physiological explanation, each applied specifically to hockey performance. The candidate links structure to function (e.g. how the femur acts as a lever at the hip during a reverse hit) and demonstrates understanding of how skeletal function supports overall performance.

Secure: Two functions are identified with mostly accurate explanation and applied to a general sporting context. Some links between structure and performance may be undeveloped.

Developing: One or two functions are mentioned with limited development. Application to sport is vague or missing from one function.

Emerging: Basic naming of functions with little or no explanation or sporting application.

Acceptable content includes: movement (long bones act as levers; femur pivots at the hip to produce the sweeping action of a reverse hit); protection (ribcage protects the heart and lungs from stick or ball impact); attachment for muscles (the scapula and pelvis provide attachment points for muscles that control the swing of the arms and legs); mineral storage (calcium stored in the skeleton maintains bone density under the repeated loading of running on hard surfaces); blood cell production (red blood cells produced in bone marrow carry oxygen to working muscles during aerobic play).

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 student says: 'The skeleton is only important for holding you upright — it doesn’t do anything else useful in sport.' How far do you agree with this statement? Evaluate the functions of the skeleton in the context of sporting performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of skeletal functions discussed with accurate physiological detail; both the role in structural support AND wider functions (protection, movement/levers, muscle attachment, mineral storage, blood cell production) are evaluated; consistent sporting examples applied throughout; candidate reaches a clear, justified conclusion that goes beyond simple support.

Secure: Most functions are covered with reasonable accuracy; sporting examples present but may not always be specific; conclusion present.

Developing: Support and one or two other functions discussed; limited sporting application; argument may be one-sided (only agreeing or disagreeing).

Emerging: Basic statement that the skeleton does more than support, but little development or sporting application.

Agreeing content: the skeleton does hold the body upright, which is essential for balance in static positions (yoga pose, balance beam, penalty kick stance); without skeletal support, the body would collapse under gravity.

Disagreeing content: the skeleton also provides protection (flat bones shield the brain and heart and lungs); movement through levers (the femur acts as a lever in running; the humerus and forearm bones produce the throwing action in cricket); attachment points for muscles (no attachment = no movement); mineral storage (calcium maintains bone strength for impact sports); blood cell production (red blood cells carry oxygen to muscles during aerobic exercise). A well-rounded athlete benefits from all six functions simultaneously.

practice_questions.text: Identify one reason why beginners are advised to avoid setting outcome goals.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of the following: winning may be unrealistic against more experienced opponents (1); repeated failure can demotivate the performer (1); outcome goals rely on factors outside the performer's control, such as the quality of opponents (1). Do not credit 'outcome goals are bad' without explanation.

practice_questions.text: State two characteristics of a performance goal.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct characteristics: it is based on personal improvement rather than the result (1); it is judged against the performer's own previous standard, not against others (1); the performer can directly influence whether the goal is achieved through their own effort and technique (1). Maximum 2 marks. Do not credit two descriptions of the same idea.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a SMART target in physical education.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly named and briefly explained element, up to 3 marks. Accept any three of: Specific — the goal is precisely defined (1); Measurable — progress can be tracked using numbers or data (1); Accepted — the goal is agreed between performer and coach (1); Realistic — the goal is challenging but achievable given current ability (1); Time-bound — the goal has a clear deadline (1). Note: mark as 'accepted' for the A — credit 'achievable' only if accompanied by a correct description.

practice_questions.text: A county-level netball player has set the following goal: 'Win the regional cup final next season.' Explain why this goal might not be effective, and suggest how it could be improved.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for the critique: the goal is an outcome goal / result-dependent (1); the player cannot control other teams' performance, referee decisions or opponent quality (1); if the team does not win, the player may feel they have failed regardless of their personal contribution, reducing motivation (1). Up to 2 marks for the improvement: a suggested performance goal e.g. 'increase interception rate from 4 to 7 per match over the next 10 games' (1); the improvement must demonstrate at least two SMART elements to earn the second mark — e.g. specific and time-bound / measurable and realistic (1).

practice_questions.text: A sports coach argues that outcome goals are always harmful to performance and should never be used. Evaluate this view, using examples from sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on both sides, each applied to a specific sporting example, with a clear and justified conclusion. Arguments in support of the coach's view: outcome goals depend on factors outside the performer's control — if a swimmer trains excellently but finishes second because of a stronger competitor, an outcome-only focus feels like failure (apply: club swimmer aiming to win county championship); for beginners, outcome goals are particularly damaging because winning against experienced opponents is unrealistic, leading to repeated demotivation and potential dropout from sport; outcome goals can increase anxiety before competition rather than focusing the performer on their own preparation. Arguments against the coach's view: outcome goals provide motivating direction for elite performers who are competing seriously for titles — knowing the target is the national championship focuses training intensity; outcome goals can be combined effectively with performance goals, so the performer has both a controllable daily target and a longer-term competitive aim; some performers are naturally outcome-oriented and respond well to competition-based targets, using a loss as a stimulus to train harder. Conclusion: outcome goals should generally be avoided or used only alongside performance goals, especially for beginners; for elite performers, a blend is most effective.

Secure: Two or three well-developed points on each side, mostly applied to sporting examples, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development; sporting context thin or inconsistent.

Emerging: One-sided response or very basic points; little or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Write a SMART target for a 16-year-old county-level javelin thrower who currently throws an average of 28 metres and wants to improve before the county championships in eight weeks.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a specific and measurable element (e.g. 'throw an average of 32 metres in the county championships' — this includes a specific distance and the named event). 1 mark for accepted/realistic element: the target is agreed with the coach and is achievable given 8 weeks of training — an increase of 4 m is challenging but realistic for a county-level athlete (1). 1 mark for time-bound element: 'within 8 weeks / before the county championships' is explicit and measurable (1). Accept alternative distances or timelines provided they are internally consistent and justified.

practice_questions.text: During a pull-up exercise, a gymnast bends her elbows to raise her body upward. Name the agonist muscle acting at the elbow joint during this upward phase.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: biceps.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'isometric contraction' and give one sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for definition: a contraction where the muscle produces tension but does not change length and no joint movement occurs; 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. gymnast holding a crucifix on the rings / rugby player in a scrum / holding a plank position).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to the quadriceps and hamstrings during the upward phase of a squat (knee extension from a bent position to standing).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the quadriceps as the agonist during knee extension; 1 mark for stating the quadriceps contracts concentrically (shortens under tension) to produce knee extension; 1 mark for stating the hamstrings act as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow the movement to occur.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between concentric and eccentric contraction, using the biceps muscle as an example in both cases.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining concentric contraction: the biceps shortens under tension during elbow flexion (upward phase of bicep curl); 1 mark for explaining eccentric contraction: the biceps lengthens under tension during elbow extension (lowering phase of bicep curl) to control the movement; 1 mark for correctly linking concentric to movement production; 1 mark for correctly linking eccentric to movement control or braking (and noting this is why DOMS can occur).

practice_questions.text: A club-level badminton player notices that her forehand smash relies on coordinated muscle action at the shoulder and elbow. Analyse the role of antagonistic muscle pairs in producing this movement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear identification of at least two antagonistic pairs relevant to the movement (e.g. deltoid/latissimus dorsi at the shoulder; triceps/biceps at the elbow); each pair discussed in terms of agonist and antagonist roles with correct contraction types (concentric/eccentric) applied to specific phases of the smash; consistent sporting application throughout; technically accurate language throughout.

Secure: Two pairs identified; mostly correct agonist/antagonist assignment; contraction types mentioned but may not be consistently linked to specific phases; generally applied to the smash.

Developing: One pair discussed with development; or two pairs identified but with limited contraction type analysis; sporting context present but superficial.

Emerging: Basic mention of agonist/antagonist with little development; incorrect assignment possible; limited sporting application.

Acceptable content: at the shoulder, the deltoid (agonist) contracts concentrically during abduction/flexion to raise the arm; the latissimus dorsi (antagonist) relaxes; at the elbow, the triceps (agonist) contracts concentrically during extension to produce the smashing action; the biceps (antagonist) relaxes and lengthens; on the follow-through, the roles reverse as the biceps contracts eccentrically to decelerate the arm.

practice_questions.text: A sprint coach claims that eccentric muscle contractions are just as important as concentric contractions for athletic performance. Evaluate this claim, referring to specific muscles and sporting actions in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation of both concentric and eccentric contractions; multiple sporting examples applied accurately; candidate demonstrates understanding of eccentric loading (DOMS, injury risk, deceleration, landing mechanics) alongside the more obvious role of concentric power production; balanced argument with a justified conclusion.

Secure: Both types discussed with relevant examples; most points accurate; conclusion present; some sporting application.

Developing: One type discussed more fully than the other; limited sporting examples; argument is one-sided.

Emerging: Basic description of contractions with little evaluation or sporting application.

Agreeing (eccentric is equally important): eccentric contractions of the hamstrings decelerate the leg after a kick, preventing knee injury; the biceps contracts eccentrically to control the lowering phase of a pull-up, building strength through a full range; the quadriceps contracts eccentrically during landing from a jump to absorb force and protect the knee; eccentric loading in plyometric training (depth jumps) maximises the stretch-shortening cycle for explosive power.

Disagreeing / partial challenge: concentric power is what drives the explosive movements in sprinting, jumping and throwing; most spectators and coaches focus on concentric strength as it directly produces performance outcomes; without concentric quadriceps power, there would be no sprint speed to decelerate.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of joint is found at the hip?
A) Hinge joint
B) Pivot joint
C) Ball-and-socket joint
D) Gliding joint
practice_questions.marks: C) Ball-and-socket joint [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: State two structures found in a synovial joint that help prevent injury.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two different valid structures: ligaments (connect bone to bone, prevent excessive movement); cartilage (absorbs compressive forces, reduces friction between bone surfaces); synovial fluid (lubricates the joint, reduces friction); bursae (cushion tendons against bone, reduce friction during repeated movement); joint capsule (encloses the joint, holds bones in position); synovial membrane (produces synovial fluid to nourish and lubricate the joint). Two near-identical answers (e.g. synovial fluid + synovial membrane without distinguishing their functions) are awarded 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of ligaments in a synovial joint during a football tackle.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that ligaments connect bone to bone across the joint; 1 mark for explaining that they limit excessive or abnormal movement, preventing joint dislocation or injury; 1 mark for applying to football (e.g. the knee ligaments prevent the tibia from moving too far sideways or forwards during a tackle, reducing the risk of ligament tear).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the shoulder joint allows a greater range of movement than the elbow joint, referring to joint type and the types of movement available at each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the shoulder as a ball-and-socket joint; 1 mark for explaining that the rounded head of the humerus fits into the cup-shaped socket of the scapula, allowing movement in all planes; 1 mark for identifying the elbow as a hinge joint; 1 mark for explaining that the pulley-shaped end of the humerus fits into the groove of the ulna, restricting movement to flexion and extension in a single plane only.

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old county swimmer performs repeated overhead arm strokes during training. Analyse how the structures of the shoulder synovial joint support performance and reduce injury risk during this activity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least two structures discussed in detail with accurate physiological explanation; each structure linked specifically to the demands of overhead swimming (e.g. bursae reducing friction as the rotator cuff tendons pass under the acromion during each stroke; synovial fluid becoming less viscous during warm-up to allow the full range of circumduction required; ligaments stabilising the ball-and-socket joint against the repetitive shoulder rotation forces); technically accurate language throughout.

Secure: Two structures identified and mostly accurately explained; applied to swimming in general terms; link between structure and performance present.

Developing: One or two structures named with limited explanation; sporting application vague.

Emerging: Basic naming of structures; little explanation of function or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A swimming coach argues that ball-and-socket joints are more beneficial for sporting performance than hinge joints. Evaluate this view, using specific sporting examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation with multiple sporting examples; both the advantages of ball-and-socket joints (range of movement) and the advantages of hinge joints (stability, power, predictability) clearly discussed; candidate reaches a nuanced conclusion acknowledging that both types are essential for different reasons.

Secure: Both joint types discussed with sporting examples; mostly accurate; conclusion reached.

Developing: One type discussed more thoroughly than the other; argument may be one-sided; sporting examples present but limited.

Emerging: Basic description of joint types; little evaluation; few sporting examples.

Agreeing: ball-and-socket joints allow movement in all directions (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, circumduction); essential for swimming (full shoulder rotation), throwing (cricket, javelin), gymnastics (full body rotation); the hip ball-and-socket allows the wide stride in sprinting and the power of a karate kick.

Disagreeing: hinge joints provide the stability needed for power generation; the knee (hinge) absorbs enormous ground-reaction forces in sprinting; the elbow (hinge) produces the precise, forceful extension in a push-up; a hinge joint that accidentally allowed sideways movement would risk catastrophic injury in contact sport; both joint types are necessary — the body needs both versatility (ball-and-socket) and stability (hinge) to perform effectively.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'selective attention' in the input stage of information processing?
A) Focusing on every piece of information in the display at once
B) Filtering out irrelevant sensory information and attending only to important cues
C) Selecting which feedback to give after a movement
D) Deciding which motor programme to use from long-term memory
practice_questions.marks: B) Filtering out irrelevant sensory information and attending only to important cues [1 mark]. Option A describes the opposite of selective attention; C describes feedback, not input; D describes decision making.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'short-term memory' as it applies to the information processing model.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: short-term memory is a temporary or working memory store that holds information while it is actively being used. 1 mark for a quality marker: it has limited capacity (approximately 7 items); it holds information for around 20-30 seconds before it fades; or it processes the current situation such as the immediate positions of players (1). Do not credit answers that confuse short-term with long-term memory.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of feedback in the information processing model, identifying one type of feedback relevant to a beginner performer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the role of feedback in the model: it provides information about the outcome or quality of the movement and feeds back into the input stage to guide future performance (1). 1 mark for identifying a feedback type relevant to beginners: extrinsic feedback (from coaches, spectators or results) / knowledge of results / knowledge of performance (1). 1 mark for explaining why it suits beginners: beginners lack proprioceptive sensitivity to rely on intrinsic feedback alone, so external information from a coach helps them correct errors they cannot feel for themselves (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the information processing model applies to a volleyball player making a dig to set up an attack. Refer to at least two stages in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per stage, maximum 4 marks across any two stages. Input: the player uses selective attention to focus on the ball's trajectory and speed, filtering out crowd noise and opponents' positions (1); their eyes and proprioceptors gather information about ball height and their own body position (1). Decision making: long-term memory retrieves the motor programme for a low dig; short-term memory identifies the position of teammates to direct the ball (1). Output: muscles of the legs, arms and shoulders coordinate to produce the digging movement, with weight transferred forward to control direction (1). Feedback: intrinsic feedback tells the player the contact was clean; extrinsic feedback from the setter confirms the height was correct (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the information processing model can explain differences between beginner and elite performers in a fast-paced sport such as basketball.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least three stages of the model clearly distinguishing beginner from elite behaviour at each stage, with specific sporting context throughout. May include: Input/selective attention — beginners struggle to filter the display and attend to irrelevant cues (the ball only) rather than teammates' runs; elite players scan the full court and rapidly attend to significant cues like an opponent's defensive position shifting. Decision making — beginners rely on conscious deliberation and have shallow long-term memory (few stored patterns), making decisions slow and often incorrect; elites retrieve complex tactical patterns instantly from extensive long-term memory, appearing to have more time. Output — beginners produce inconsistent output because the motor programme is poorly established; elites execute fluid, automatic movements. Feedback — beginners depend on extrinsic feedback from coaches because intrinsic proprioceptive feedback is not yet calibrated; elites self-correct in real time using intrinsic feel. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure: Three stages addressed with accurate distinctions and some sporting context. May be less precise on one stage.

Developing: Two stages addressed; distinction between beginner and elite present but underdeveloped; limited sporting context.

Emerging: Stages named but not developed; little or no beginner/elite distinction.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old goalkeeper is learning to face penalty kicks. In training, she faces 20 penalties per session. Evaluate whether improving the input and decision making stages of information processing is more important than improving her output stage for reducing goals conceded.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, consistently applied to the goalkeeper scenario, with a justified conclusion. Arguments that input/decision making matters more: a goalkeeper who cannot read the penalty taker's body language and ball placement cues (input failure) will dive the wrong way regardless of how athletic her dive is; improving selective attention — scanning the run-up angle, non-kicking foot position and hips — could allow her to predict ball direction before contact, narrowing the decision to two or three options; long-term memory stores patterns of penalty takers' preferred side, giving experienced keepers a significant edge at the decision making stage; elite goalkeepers make save decisions largely in the input and decision-making stage — by the time the ball is struck, output is largely reactive. Arguments that output matters more: even correct anticipation is wasted if the diving technique is slow, mistimed or lacking reach; explosive leg drive (output quality) allows the goalkeeper to cover more of the goal even with a less precise prediction; at top speed, the reaction time window means input and decision making have minimal time — output athleticism becomes the decisive factor. Justified conclusion: both stages are interdependent; at beginner level, improving input quality (reading cues) may yield the bigger gain, but output athleticism limits the ceiling of what input improvement can achieve.

Secure: Two or three developed points on each side, mostly applied to the goalkeeper scenario, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development or thin sporting application; may be one-sided.

Emerging: Basic response with little development; may describe stages rather than evaluate them.

practice_questions.text: Name the vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: pulmonary vein.

practice_questions.text: During a 5 km race, a runner has a heart rate of 160 bpm and a stroke volume of 95 ml. Calculate her cardiac output. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct formula and substitution: Q = stroke volume × heart rate = 95 ml × 160 bpm; 1 mark for correct answer with unit: 15,200 ml/min (or 15.2 L/min). If the answer is correct but the unit is missing, award 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of arteries and explain how this structure relates to their function.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that arteries have thick, muscular and elastic walls; 1 mark for explaining that thick walls are needed to withstand the high pressure generated by the ventricle contracting; 1 mark for explaining that elastic walls allow the vessel to stretch and recoil with each heartbeat, smoothing blood flow and helping maintain pressure between beats.

practice_questions.text: Explain how vasoconstriction and vasodilation work together to meet the increased oxygen demands of working muscles during a sprint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining vasodilation: the widening of blood vessels supplying the active muscles, increasing blood flow; 1 mark for defining vasoconstriction: the narrowing of blood vessels supplying inactive areas (e.g. digestive system, skin), reducing blood flow there; 1 mark for explaining that this redistribution channels more blood (and therefore oxygen) to the working muscles; 1 mark for applying to sprinting (e.g. the leg muscles receive a much greater share of the total cardiac output during a sprint, meeting the high ATP demand for explosive contraction).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows data for a trained cyclist at rest and during a 20-minute time trial. Resting: heart rate 48 bpm, stroke volume 85 ml. During time trial: heart rate 172 bpm, stroke volume 115 ml. Calculate the cardiac output at rest and during the time trial, and interpret what the data tells you about the physiological demands of a cycling time trial.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct resting cardiac output: 48 × 85 = 4,080 ml/min; 1 mark for correct exercise cardiac output: 172 × 115 = 19,780 ml/min; 1 mark for a valid comparison using both figures (e.g. cardiac output increases by approximately 15,700 ml/min during the time trial — almost five times the resting value); 1 mark for an explanation of the sporting implication (e.g. the dramatic increase in cardiac output reflects the greatly elevated oxygen demand of the working leg muscles during sustained high-intensity cycling; the trained athlete’s low resting heart rate and high stroke volume indicate a strong, efficient heart capable of meeting this demand). If calculations are incorrect but method is sound, award 1 mark for working and 1 mark for a valid interpretation of their calculated figures.

practice_questions.text: A weekend footballer is considering whether to add cardiovascular training to his programme. Evaluate the importance of the cardiovascular system to his performance in a 90-minute match, using your knowledge of heart structure, blood vessels and the responses to exercise.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of content covered with accuracy — heart chambers and their roles, cardiac output calculation applied to exercise demand, blood vessel functions, vasoconstriction/vasodilation, anticipatory rise and recovery curve; all applied specifically and consistently to a 90-minute football match; balanced evaluation (importance acknowledged with detail, plus limitations or individual variation considered); clear justified conclusion.

Secure: Most cardiovascular structures and responses covered with reasonable accuracy; applied to football; conclusion reached; some minor inaccuracies or undeveloped points.

Developing: Cardiovascular system described with limited application to football; cardiac output mentioned but may not be calculated; one-sided (either all positive or missing evaluation of how CV fitness affects football performance).

Emerging: Basic points about heart rate increasing during exercise; limited structure or sporting application.

Content pointers: heart rate rises from resting ~72 bpm to 170–185 bpm during high-intensity phases; cardiac output increases from ~5 L/min at rest to over 20 L/min during sprints; vasodilation delivers more oxygen to the leg and core muscles during attacking runs; vasoconstriction reduces blood supply to non-essential organs; capillary networks in working muscles allow gas exchange; a high stroke volume (trained heart) means the footballer’s heart does not have to beat as fast to deliver the same cardiac output, delaying fatigue; a trained CV system also supports faster recovery between high-intensity sprints within the match.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of guidance being used when a gymnastics coach physically moves a learner's arms through the correct cartwheel pattern.
practice_questions.marks: Manual guidance [1 mark]. The coach is physically assisting the performer's movement through direct physical contact.

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using visual guidance when coaching a beginner.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct advantages: it provides a complete mental image/model of the skill, giving beginners a blueprint of the correct movement pattern (1); it is easy to understand without prior knowledge of the skill (1); it can demonstrate the whole skill in context rather than describing it in abstract terms (1); video can be replayed, paused and slowed down for detailed analysis (1). Maximum 2 marks; do not credit the same point twice with different wording.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a swimming coach could use mechanical guidance when teaching a beginner to swim front crawl, and explain one disadvantage of this approach.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for an accurate description of mechanical guidance in context: the coach uses armbands or floats / a pull buoy / a lane rope to support the swimmer's body position, allowing them to focus on arm technique while the device provides buoyancy (1). 1 mark for identifying a disadvantage: the swimmer may become reliant on the float/armband (1). 1 mark for developing the disadvantage: without the aid, the swimmer has not learned to control their own buoyancy, which is a fundamental skill needed for independent swimming (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why verbal guidance is more effective for an elite javelin thrower than for a beginner. Use your knowledge of how each performer uses memory in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for explaining effectiveness for the elite performer: the elite athlete has an established, detailed movement pattern stored in long-term memory (1); a single precise verbal cue (e.g. 'release later') activates and fine-tunes this existing pattern without disrupting the automatic flow of the skill (1). Up to 2 marks for explaining the limitation for a beginner: the beginner has no stored movement programme in long-term memory (1); they cannot translate abstract verbal instructions into coordinated physical movement without first experiencing or seeing the skill, so verbal guidance alone provides insufficient information to perform the skill (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level athletics coach is deciding which types of guidance to use with two performers: a Year-7 beginner learning the shot-put for the first time, and a county-level sixth-form athlete preparing for a regional competition. Analyse how the coach should use guidance differently for each performer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least three guidance types across the two performers, with clear justifications rooted in stage of learning and sporting context. Consistently distinguishes between the two performers throughout. May include: Visual guidance — for the beginner, a full demonstration of the correct put action provides a mental model they have no experience of; for the elite athlete, video analysis of their release angle can reveal subtle technical faults. Verbal guidance — limited use for the beginner because they lack an existing movement programme to attach cues to; highly effective for the elite athlete who can translate a brief cue ('extend the glide phase') into a physical adjustment. Manual guidance — appropriate for the beginner to give the correct kinaesthetic feel for the stance and wrist position; inappropriate for the elite athlete as it disrupts their automatic motor programme. Mechanical guidance — beginners may use a lighter shot or a target circle marked on the ground to constrain practice conditions safely; elite athletes rarely need mechanical guidance. Evaluates the balance rather than listing.

Secure: Three guidance types discussed with mostly accurate justification. Distinguishes between performers on at least two types.

Developing: Two guidance types with some justification; may be less clear on why the difference exists between beginner and elite.

Emerging: One or two types named with little justification; may not distinguish between performers.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club trampolinist is learning a new double somersault. Her coach uses a safety harness during initial practice sessions. Evaluate whether mechanical guidance is always the most appropriate form of guidance when teaching new acrobatic skills, referring to both its benefits and limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, consistently applied to the trampolinist scenario and/or other acrobatic sporting examples, with a justified conclusion. Arguments in support of mechanical guidance: the safety harness allows the athlete to experience the correct rotation of a double somersault without risk of injury; the physical sensation (kinaesthetic feel) from being supported through the skill provides information about the required body position that verbal description could not convey; it builds confidence in a dangerous skill so the performer is not held back by fear; mechanical guidance reduces the risk of reinforcing incorrect patterns by preventing unsafe improvisations. Arguments against / limitations: over-reliance on the harness creates dependency; the trampolinist may fail to develop the internal body control and timing needed to perform unsupported; the harness may alter the feel of the skill slightly, meaning the athlete must still adjust when performing without it; other guidance types may be more appropriate in combination, such as verbal cues ('tuck tighter') and video analysis of existing attempts; for skills with lower danger levels, manual or visual guidance may be equally effective without the dependency risk. Justified conclusion: mechanical guidance is most justified in high-risk acrobatic skills during the early learning phase, but should be progressively withdrawn as competence develops, and combined with verbal and visual guidance for complete skill acquisition.

Secure: Two or three developed points on each side, mostly applied to the sporting scenario, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but underdeveloped; sporting context present but thin or one-sided.

Emerging: Basic response; may list guidance types without evaluating mechanical guidance specifically.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes knowledge of performance?
A) The time taken to complete a race
B) The score achieved in a gymnastics routine
C) The technical quality of the movements used to produce an outcome
D) The crowd reaction to an athlete's performance
practice_questions.marks: C) The technical quality of the movements used to produce an outcome [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'intrinsic feedback'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that intrinsic feedback comes from within the performer / the performer's own body / senses; 1 mark for naming the sensory mechanism involved (proprioception / kinaesthetic sense / sight / touch) or stating it is received during or immediately after movement. Example: 'Intrinsic feedback is information received from within the performer's own body — through proprioception and other senses — about how a movement felt during or immediately after its execution.'

practice_questions.text: Describe how knowledge of results and knowledge of performance each help an athlete improve. Use a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining knowledge of results — information about the outcome (score, time, distance) that tells the performer whether they succeeded or not; 1 mark for explaining knowledge of performance — information about the quality of the movement or technique used, pointing to what needs to change; 1 mark for a relevant sporting example that illustrates either or both (e.g. a high jumper learning their bar clearance height is KR, while being told their Fosbury flop arch needs to be higher is KP).

practice_questions.text: Explain why positive feedback is particularly important for beginner performers in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining positive feedback as information that tells the performer what they did correctly; 1 mark for explaining that it reinforces the correct movement pattern in memory, making repetition more likely; 1 mark for linking to the beginner context — beginners make frequent errors and their confidence and motivation can be fragile, so reinforcing what is right encourages continued participation; 1 mark for a specific sporting example or further development (e.g. a beginner swimmer is told 'your arm entry was straight' — this confirms a technique she should repeat and helps her build a reliable kinaesthetic reference point).

practice_questions.text: A volleyball coach is working with two different groups: a Year 7 class learning to serve for the first time, and a county under-18 team preparing for a regional final. Analyse how the coach should adapt the type and focus of feedback given to each group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains at least two contrasting feedback strategies for each group, linking each to a specific reason grounded in the difference between beginners and elite performers. Applies consistent sporting examples to the volleyball context. Recognises that feedback type (positive/negative, intrinsic/extrinsic, KR/KP) varies systematically with experience level. Writes in developed prose rather than bullet points.

Secure: Identifies appropriate feedback for each group with some explanation. At least one reference to a specific feedback type (e.g. KP more useful for elite). Sporting application present but may be brief.

Developing: Makes relevant points about beginners needing simpler or more encouraging feedback, but development is limited. May describe rather than analyse. Sporting application minimal or absent.

Emerging: Basic points only (e.g. 'give more positive feedback to beginners'). No sporting application and limited development.

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old county-level javelin thrower is told by his coach: 'Your run-up speed was good, but your elbow dropped below shoulder height at release — that cost you distance.' Identify and explain two types of feedback present in this statement.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that positive feedback is present ('run-up speed was good'); 1 mark for explaining that this reinforces the correct run-up technique so the athlete repeats it; 1 mark for identifying that negative feedback is present ('elbow dropped below shoulder height') or that knowledge of performance is present (the feedback is about technique quality not outcome); 1 mark for explaining that this gives the performer a specific technical target to correct in the next throw. (Accept identification of extrinsic feedback and explanation that it comes from the coach, not from the athlete's own sensations.)

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct order of the air pathway from the trachea to the site of gaseous exchange?
A) Trachea → alveoli → bronchi → bronchioles
B) Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
C) Trachea → bronchioles → bronchi → alveoli
D) Trachea → alveoli → bronchioles → bronchi
practice_questions.marks: B) Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'tidal volume'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying tidal volume as a measure of air volume per breath; 1 mark for specifying it is the volume inhaled or exhaled in a single normal breath (accept: approximately 0.5 litres at rest).

practice_questions.text: Describe three structural features of the alveoli that make gaseous exchange efficient.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of the following: large surface area of the alveoli; moist, thin walls (one cell thick); short diffusion distance/pathway; large capillary network surrounding the alveoli; large blood supply; concentration gradient is maintained (oxygen high in alveoli, low in blood; CO2 high in blood, low in alveoli). Accept equivalent wording.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club swimmer trains four days per week at high intensity. Explain how her breathing mechanics change during a maximal swim effort compared with breathing at rest.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that breathing rate increases during exercise; 1 mark for explaining that tidal volume increases (deeper breaths); 1 mark for naming an accessory inspiratory muscle (pectorals or sternocleidomastoid) that assists inhalation; 1 mark for explaining that abdominal muscles actively contract on exhalation to force air out more rapidly (compared with passive exhalation at rest). Partial credit: 3 marks for any three of these points accurately explained.

practice_questions.text: A county-level middle-distance runner is preparing for a regional 1500 m race. Analyse how the structure of the respiratory system allows her to maintain a sufficient supply of oxygen to her muscles throughout the race.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed, well-developed response that links several structural features of the respiratory system (alveolar structure, diffusion gradient, capillary network) to sustained oxygen delivery during the race. Each point is applied to the running context and explained mechanistically. Accurate use of terms such as diffusion, concentration gradient, haemoglobin, tidal volume and minute ventilation.

Secure (3-4 marks): Most key points present and generally accurate. Structural features are identified and broadly linked to the race context, though some points may be stated rather than fully explained. Most technical vocabulary used correctly.

Developing (2 marks): Relevant points made about the pathway of air or alveolar features, but development is limited. May list features without explaining how they help the runner. Some inaccuracy in terminology.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic correct point about the respiratory system or breathing during exercise, with little or no application to the racing context.

practice_questions.text: A Year-10 student claims that oxygen automatically moves into the blood simply because we breathe in. Critically examine whether this statement is accurate, and explain the process by which oxygen actually enters the bloodstream from the alveoli.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear identification that the student's statement is oversimplified. Full explanation of diffusion as the mechanism (movement from high to low concentration); concentration gradients specified (high O2 in alveolus, low O2 in blood); haemoglobin's role in binding oxygen named; structural features of the alveoli linked to the efficiency of diffusion. The critique of the original statement is precise and evidence-based.

Secure (3-4 marks): Identifies diffusion as the process, provides accurate concentration gradient explanation, and names at least one structural feature. Critique of the statement present but may be partial.

Developing (2 marks): Mentions diffusion or concentration gradient but does not fully explain the process. Structural features may be missing. Critique of the statement is weak or implied only.

Emerging (1 mark): Recognises that something happens at the alveoli to allow oxygen to enter the blood, but lacks precise explanation.

practice_questions.text: Identify the term used to describe the arousal level at which performance is at its highest on the inverted-U graph.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for 'optimal arousal' or equivalent (e.g. 'optimum arousal', 'peak arousal point').

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'arousal' in the context of sporting performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a physical dimension of arousal (e.g. increased heart rate, heightened muscle tension, physical readiness); 1 mark for identifying a mental/psychological dimension (e.g. alertness, mental readiness, state of activation). A definition that addresses only one dimension earns 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the inverted-U theory explains what happens to performance when a competitor is over-aroused.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that arousal has risen beyond the optimal point on the curve; 1 mark for describing the effect on performance (performance decreases / deteriorates / drops from its peak); 1 mark for identifying a mechanism or example (e.g. fine motor control breaks down, decision making deteriorates, anxiety increases, choking occurs under pressure — or a specific sport example such as a tennis player double-faulting due to excess nerves).

practice_questions.text: A club-level archer is preparing for a county championship and tells her coach she feels 'absolutely terrified'. Explain how mental rehearsal could help her manage her arousal before she shoots.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that mental rehearsal / visualisation / imagery is a stress management technique; 1 mark for explaining what it involves (creating a detailed internal image of successfully executing the skill, using all senses, first-person perspective); 1 mark for linking to arousal reduction (activating the same neural pathways as physical practice, building confidence, reducing cognitive anxiety); 1 mark for specific application to the archery context (e.g. she visualises drawing the bow, holding, releasing and the arrow striking the gold, building the feeling that she has 'been here before').

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level sprinter competes well in training but consistently underperforms in major competitions. Her coach believes she becomes over-aroused on race day. Analyse the stress management techniques available to the sprinter and how each could help her return to optimal arousal.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses all three techniques (deep breathing, mental rehearsal, positive self-talk) with a clear explanation of how each works physiologically or psychologically, and specific application to the sprinter's situation. Evaluates which technique(s) suit the timing of arousal management (pre-race vs on-the-blocks). Recognises that sprinting is a gross skill and therefore the optimal arousal point is higher than for a fine skill, meaning only modest reduction is needed.

Secure: Covers at least two techniques with explanation of mechanism and sporting application. May not evaluate timing or skill-type suitability. Some analysis rather than pure description.

Developing: Names two or more techniques and briefly explains one. Limited application to the sprinter specifically. Mostly descriptive.

Emerging: Names one technique with limited explanation. No sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that the inverted-U theory fully explains the relationship between arousal and performance in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a balanced evaluation with well-developed points on both sides. Arguments in support: the theory correctly predicts that both under- and over-arousal reduce performance; it accounts for skill-type variation (gross vs fine); it provides coaches with a practical framework for monitoring and adjusting arousal. Arguments against or limitations: the theory assumes a single smooth peak for all tasks and all athletes, but individual differences (personality type — introvert vs extrovert, experience level) mean the curve shifts position; the theory does not explain why some athletes 'choke' catastrophically rather than declining gradually. Reaches a justified conclusion. Uses sporting examples throughout.

Secure: Presents both sides with some development. At least one limitation identified. Sporting examples present. May not fully balance both sides or justify the conclusion.

Developing: Mostly one-sided (either supporting or criticising the theory). Some relevant points but limited development. Sporting application may be absent.

Emerging: Basic points only, largely descriptive. No meaningful balance.

practice_questions.text: Identify whether the following activity is aerobic or anaerobic: a boxer throwing a 15-second combination of punches at maximum intensity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: anaerobic. Accept: anaerobic exercise / uses the anaerobic pathway. Do not accept 'aerobic' for full credit.

practice_questions.text: Define the term EPOC.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying EPOC as excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (or the oxygen debt); 1 mark for explaining that it is the elevated oxygen uptake after exercise used to remove lactic acid and restore the body to its resting state.

practice_questions.text: A club-level hockey player completes a hard training session. Explain how a cool down helps her body recover from the session.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the cool down maintains an elevated heart rate and breathing rate; 1 mark for explaining that this keeps blood flowing through the muscles; 1 mark for stating this continued blood flow delivers oxygen to the muscles; 1 mark for explaining that this oxygen is used to remove/process lactic acid produced during the session (or: that it helps repay the oxygen debt/EPOC). Partial credit: 3 marks for any three of these points accurately explained.

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 sprinter completes a 200 m time trial. Analyse why this activity is primarily anaerobic and explain the physiological consequences she is likely to experience in the minutes immediately after finishing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear identification that a 200 m sprint involves very high intensity over approximately 20-25 seconds, meaning oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough for aerobic respiration alone. Glucose → energy + lactic acid explained. Lactic acid accumulation linked to fatigue and the burning sensation during the effort. Post-exercise: EPOC defined and linked to sustained elevated breathing, with the purpose of removing lactic acid and restoring oxygen stores explained. Sporting context (the sprint distance and intensity) woven throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): Anaerobic identification with brief justification; lactic acid named; EPOC described with at least one purpose. Most points accurate but may lack development or sporting application.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies the activity as anaerobic; mentions lactic acid or EPOC but does not explain the mechanism. Limited or no sporting application.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic correct point, such as identifying the activity as anaerobic or naming lactic acid, with no developed explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of ice baths and cool down as recovery methods for a competitive swimmer who trains twice a day during a major competition block.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): Balanced, well-developed evaluation of both methods with clear sporting application to the twice-daily training context. Cool down: advantages (maintains blood flow, removes lactic acid, reduces muscle tightness); limitations (time-consuming between sessions; reduces available recovery window when training is twice daily). Ice baths: advantages (reduces inflammation and DOMS between sessions, particularly valuable when recovery time is short); limitations (discomfort, access in pool environments, some evidence suggests they may blunt training adaptations if used too frequently). Candidate reaches a justified conclusion about which method is most valuable for this specific context.

Secure (5-7 marks): Both methods addressed with relevant advantages and disadvantages. Sporting application to swimming competition context mostly present. Minor gaps in development or balance.

Developing (3-4 marks): One method covered well, or both methods described with limited evaluation. Sporting application present but limited. One-sided or descriptive rather than analytical.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about one or both methods. Little or no evaluation. Minimal sporting application.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between aerobic and anaerobic exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct differences, for example: aerobic uses oxygen / anaerobic does not use sufficient oxygen; aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water / anaerobic produces lactic acid; aerobic can be sustained for longer / anaerobic is short duration; aerobic is lower intensity / anaerobic is very high intensity. Accept equivalent wording. Do not award two marks for the same physiological point expressed differently.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes an extrovert?
A) Quiet, thoughtful, prefers individual sports
B) Sociable, talkative, prone to boredom when isolated
C) Motivated by personal achievement rather than rewards
D) Requires low arousal to perform at their best
practice_questions.marks: B) Sociable, talkative, prone to boredom when isolated [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'intrinsic motivation' and give one example from sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a definition that identifies intrinsic motivation as coming from within the performer / driven by personal satisfaction, enjoyment or pride in the activity itself; 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. a runner who trains because she loves the feeling of a personal best, a footballer who plays because of his enjoyment of the game rather than for prize money).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between direct and indirect aggression in sport. Give one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining that direct aggression involves physical contact with the opponent; 1 mark for explaining that indirect aggression involves force directed through an object without physical contact with the opponent; 1 mark for a valid example of each (direct: a rugby tackle, a martial arts throw, a body check in ice hockey; indirect: a fast bowler's short-pitched delivery, a smash in badminton aimed at the opponent, a hard drive in hockey).

practice_questions.text: A junior athletics coach uses medals and trophies to reward young athletes at every club competition. Explain how this approach could both benefit and harm the athletes' long-term motivation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that medals and trophies are tangible extrinsic rewards; 1 mark for explaining the benefit — they provide short-term motivation, keep young athletes engaged and celebrate achievement, which helps maintain participation at the early stage of development; 1 mark for explaining the potential harm — overuse of extrinsic rewards can cause the athlete to become dependent on them, so that if rewards are reduced or removed motivation and participation drop; 1 mark for linking to intrinsic motivation — excessive extrinsic rewards may crowd out or undermine the internal enjoyment that would sustain long-term participation.

practice_questions.text: A year-10 student who is naturally introverted joins both a swimming club and a football team. Analyse how her personality type is likely to affect her experience, performance and motivation in each sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies introvert characteristics (quiet, thoughtful, prefers concentration, enjoys solitude, lower optimal arousal) and applies them consistently to both sports. Explains why swimming suits the introvert (individual, precision-focused, lower social demand, lower arousal environment), and why football may present challenges (team environment, high external stimulation, faster pace, gross skills, social demands). Links to motivation — intrinsic motivation more likely in swimming; football may require more extrinsic support. Developed prose, sporting examples throughout.

Secure: Identifies relevant introvert characteristics and applies to at least one sport well. Some analysis rather than pure description. Arousal or motivation linked to personality.

Developing: Names introvert characteristics correctly but applies them in a limited way. May describe sports without clearly linking personality traits to sporting performance or motivation.

Emerging: Basic points only. Little or no application of personality to sport.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the view that extrinsic motivation is more effective than intrinsic motivation in encouraging long-term participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument with well-developed points on both sides. Arguments supporting extrinsic effectiveness: provides immediate, visible rewards that beginners and younger participants can relate to; tangible rewards (medals, trophies) and intangible rewards (praise, recognition) can sustain engagement through difficult periods; extrinsic rewards can trigger feelings of pride and self-satisfaction that themselves develop intrinsic enjoyment. Arguments against: intrinsic motivation is more durable because it is not dependent on external provision; overuse of extrinsic rewards risks dependency — if removed, motivation drops sharply (overjustification effect); performers motivated intrinsically are more resilient when results are poor. Justified conclusion reached. Sporting examples used throughout (e.g. a club footballer who stops playing when no longer selected for awards vs a runner who trains through winter because she loves it).

Secure: Both sides represented with some development. At least one limitation of extrinsic motivation acknowledged. Sporting examples present. Conclusion present but may be undeveloped.

Developing: Mostly one-sided. Some relevant points but limited development. Little sporting application.

Emerging: Basic points only, largely descriptive. No meaningful balance.

practice_questions.text: Identify one immediate effect of exercise on the body.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: increased heart rate; increased breathing rate/depth; hot, sweaty or red skin. Accept equivalent physiological descriptions.

practice_questions.text: State two short-term effects of exercise that may appear within 36 hours of a training session.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct short-term effects from: tiredness/fatigue; light-headedness; nausea; aching muscles; DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness); cramp. Do not accept 'increased heart rate' (immediate effect). Award once for the same point expressed differently.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the resting heart rates of three athletes before and after a 6-month endurance training programme.

Athlete | Resting HR before (bpm) | Resting HR after (bpm)
Alex   | 74                      | 61
Beth   | 68                      | 55
Carlos | 72                      | 58

Calculate the mean reduction in resting heart rate across all three athletes. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly calculating each individual reduction (Alex: 13 bpm; Beth: 13 bpm; Carlos: 14 bpm); 1 mark for summing correctly (13 + 13 + 14 = 40 bpm) and dividing by 3; 1 mark for the correct final answer: 13.3 bpm (accept 13 or 13.3). Units required (bpm) for the final answer mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain how cardiac hypertrophy leads to bradycardia in a trained endurance athlete.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining cardiac hypertrophy as the long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle due to training; 1 mark for explaining that this means the heart can pump a greater stroke volume per beat; 1 mark for explaining that a higher stroke volume means the heart beats fewer times to deliver the same cardiac output; 1 mark for naming or defining bradycardia as a lower resting heart rate (below normal, typically below 60 bpm in trained athletes). Full marks require the logical chain to be clear.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level basketball player has been following a structured fitness programme for eight months. Analyse the long-term physiological effects this programme is likely to have had on her body, and how these effects might improve her performance on court.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Detailed, well-developed response identifying multiple long-term effects (cardiac hypertrophy, bradycardia, muscular hypertrophy, improved muscular endurance/strength/speed, possible changes to body composition). Each adaptation is linked to a mechanism (e.g. cardiac hypertrophy increases stroke volume, lowering resting HR) and then to a specific basketball performance benefit (e.g. sustained cardiovascular output across four quarters; greater explosive power for jumping). Technically accurate language used throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): Most key long-term effects identified with generally accurate explanations. At least one adaptation linked to a basketball context. May lack development on mechanisms.

Developing (2 marks): One or two long-term effects mentioned but not fully explained. Limited sporting application to basketball.

Emerging (1 mark): A basic correct point about a long-term effect (e.g. the heart gets bigger) with little or no explanation or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A club runner claims that feeling sore the day after a hard run means she has overtrained and should rest completely. Evaluate whether this claim is accurate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear identification of DOMS and its mechanism (micro-tears in muscle fibres, especially from eccentric contractions). Explains that DOMS is a normal, expected short-term effect rather than a sign of overtraining. Discusses when DOMS is benign (manageable soreness, peaks 24-48 hours) vs when it signals overtraining (severe, persistent, affecting movement). Considers both sides: complete rest is not always necessary — light activity, massage or ice baths can manage DOMS while allowing recovery; but if soreness is extreme or persistent, rest is warranted. Justified conclusion reached.

Secure (3-4 marks): DOMS explained correctly; the claim is challenged with some justification. Some appreciation of both sides (DOMS is normal; severe cases need rest). Sporting context present.

Developing (2 marks): DOMS mentioned but not well explained. Limited evaluation — may agree or disagree with the statement without full justification.

Emerging (1 mark): Identifies DOMS or muscle soreness as the relevant concept but provides little analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Which class of lever is used when a gymnast rises onto the tips of her toes (plantar flexion at the ankle)?
A) First class lever — the fulcrum is between the load and the effort
B) Second class lever — the load is between the fulcrum and the effort
C) Third class lever — the effort is between the fulcrum and the load
D) Second class lever — the effort is between the fulcrum and the load
practice_questions.marks: B) Second class lever — the load is between the fulcrum and the effort [1 mark]. The ball of the foot = fulcrum, body weight at the ankle = load, gastrocnemius pulling at the heel = effort.

practice_questions.text: A rugby player's forearm acts as a lever during elbow flexion. The effort arm (elbow joint to biceps insertion) measures 4 cm and the load arm (elbow joint to ball being caught) measures 36 cm. Calculate the mechanical advantage of this lever.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct substitution into the formula: mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm = 4 ÷ 36; 1 mark for the correct answer: 0.11 (accept 0.1 or 1/9). Units: the answer is dimensionless (no unit needed, but lengths must be in the same unit). The arm lengths must be in the same unit — if a student uses different units (cm vs m) without converting, award method mark only if the formula is correctly applied.

practice_questions.text: Describe the first class lever used when a swimmer performs a push-back stroke, focusing on elbow extension. Name all three components and their positions.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the fulcrum as the elbow joint; 1 mark for identifying the effort as the triceps muscle force (pulling on the olecranon behind the elbow); 1 mark for identifying the load as the weight of the forearm/hand/water resistance (in front of the elbow joint), with the fulcrum correctly placed between load and effort. Award full credit only if the positions confirm a first class arrangement (fulcrum between load and effort).

practice_questions.text: A sports coach tells a group of young athletes: 'Most of your throwing and striking actions are inefficient because the effort arm is shorter than the load arm.' Explain why this is not necessarily a limitation, and how the lever arrangement in throwing actually benefits performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the throwing action uses a third class lever (effort between fulcrum and load); 1 mark for explaining that when the effort arm is shorter than the load arm, mechanical advantage is less than 1; 1 mark for explaining that this mechanical disadvantage is compensated by an amplification of speed — a small muscular shortening produces a large movement of the hand; 1 mark for applying to throwing: the high speed of hand movement produced by the third class lever allows the athlete to throw the object with greater velocity than a lever with MA > 1 would generate. Accept equivalent reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the three classes of lever are each used in sport, explaining how the mechanical advantage of each influences the type of movement it is best suited to.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): All three lever classes correctly identified with accurate sporting examples. The mechanism and position of F, L and E described for each. Mechanical advantage for each class linked to a clear explanation of the movement advantage it provides: first class (variable MA, can favour force or speed depending on positions — e.g. head nodding); second class (MA > 1, force amplified — plantar flexion, good for lifting body weight); third class (MA < 1, speed amplified — elbow flexion, throwing, good for striking/catching). Explanations developed and clearly connected to sporting performance.

Secure (3-4 marks): At least two lever classes correctly described with sporting examples and a link to mechanical advantage. Minor inaccuracies or missing development on one class.

Developing (2 marks): One or two lever classes described; limited understanding of mechanical advantage or sporting application.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one lever class or provides a basic description without full component labelling or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A sprinter's ankle joint acts as a lever during the push-off phase of a running stride. The effort arm measures 7 cm and the load arm measures 4 cm. Calculate the mechanical advantage and state what this tells you about the type of force this lever produces.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: MA = 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75; 1 mark for correct interpretation: MA > 1 means force is amplified (this lever has a mechanical advantage — the calf muscles can lift the body weight with less effort than the weight itself). Accept: this is a second class lever that favours force production.

practice_questions.text: Identify one factor related to media coverage that could reduce female participation in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid response linking media coverage to reduced female participation, e.g.: women's sport receives less broadcast time than men's sport, reducing the visibility of female role models; lack of media coverage means female sport is perceived as less important or prestigious; girls are less likely to see women competing and therefore less likely to aspire to participate.

practice_questions.text: State two factors related to disability that can reduce a person's participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid factor, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: inaccessible facilities (e.g. no ramps, no hoist equipment in pools); lack of adapted equipment; absence of disability-specific coaching sessions; negative stereotyping by coaches or institutions; attitudinal barriers (assumptions that disabled people are not interested in or capable of sport); lack of role models in disability sport.

practice_questions.text: Describe how socio-economic factors can affect engagement patterns in physical activity. Give an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining or explaining what socio-economic factors are (related to income, social class, occupation — factors that affect disposable income and available leisure time); 1 mark for explaining the mechanism — lower income means less money for club memberships, equipment, transport or specialist coaching, making sport less accessible; 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. a family with limited income cannot afford football club fees, sports kit or travel to away fixtures; free-to-use community sport programmes are therefore critical).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows participation in organised sport among four social groups at a secondary school over one term.

Group | Participation rate
Male students | 68%
Female students | 41%
Students with a disability | 22%
Students from lower socio-economic backgrounds | 35%
