Using the data in Table 1, interpret what the data shows about engagement patterns at this school and suggest one reason for the lowest participation rate shown.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the lowest participation group (students with a disability, 22%); 1 mark for making a valid comparison using figures (e.g. students with a disability participate at 22% compared to 68% for male students — a gap of 46 percentage points); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (disabled students are significantly less likely to participate in organised sport, suggesting barriers to access or inclusion at this school); 1 mark for suggesting one valid reason for the low rate (inaccessible facilities, lack of adapted provision, attitudinal barriers from staff or peers, negative stereotyping, absence of disability sport sessions or role models).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the factors that explain why engagement patterns in physical activity differ between older adults (aged 60+) and young adults (aged 18–30).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains at least three contrasting factors across both age groups, applying each specifically to the age group. For older adults: physical decline (reduced strength, flexibility, cardiovascular endurance, increased injury risk), fewer social networks, reduced available provision, negative stereotypes about ageing and sport, reduced leisure time in pre-retirement years. For young adults: transition out of compulsory education removes structured activity, competing demands of work and family reduce leisure time, dropout cliff phenomenon as sport becomes optional. Recognises enabling factors for older adults (walking football, aqua aerobics, adapted provision). Developed prose with sporting examples.

Secure: Addresses both age groups with at least two factors per group and some explanation of mechanism. Sporting application present. May lack full balance or detailed development.

Developing: Identifies relevant factors but treats them superficially. May focus on only one age group or list without explanation. Sporting context limited.

Emerging: Basic points only. Little age-specific application.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which role models are the most important factor in improving engagement patterns among under-represented groups in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced evaluation with well-developed points on both sides. Arguments in support: positive role models give under-represented groups aspirational figures who look like them, demonstrating that sport is possible (e.g. Beth Mead and women's football registrations, Dame Sarah Storey and disability sport); they increase media coverage indirectly by making their sport more commercially attractive; they challenge stereotypes that deter participation. Arguments against or limitations: role models alone cannot overcome structural barriers such as inaccessible facilities, socio-economic cost, scheduling conflicts related to religion or family, or institutionalised discrimination; media coverage and accessibility are arguably more systemic levers; without affordable, accessible provision, a role model's inspiration cannot translate into actual participation. Justified conclusion reached, e.g. role models are necessary but insufficient — they must be accompanied by structural changes in access and provision. Sporting examples throughout.

Secure: Both sides with some development. At least one limitation of relying solely on role models identified. Conclusion present. Examples used.

Developing: Mostly one-sided. Some relevant points but limited development. Sporting application limited.

Emerging: Basic, largely descriptive. No meaningful balance or evaluation.

before.exam_tip_html: On a 4 marks — Interpret Data question about engagement patterns, you must do three things: quote a specific figure from the data, make a comparison, and explain what it means in a sporting context. Simply reading a number off a table earns nothing by itself — the mark scheme rewards the inference. For example: “School B has 27% participation compared to School A’s 18% — a difference of 9 percentage points — suggesting School B has more inclusive provision or stronger role model visibility.” On a 9 marks — Evaluate question about factors affecting engagement, a common error is listing only one group’s barriers. Full marks require multiple factors applied across different groups, with balanced points (both barriers and enabling factors), sporting examples and a justified conclusion. Use the cross-cutting factors (role models, media, socio-economic access) as a framework to structure a balanced answer.

practice_questions.text: Identify the plane of movement used during a forward somersault.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: sagittal plane.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'longitudinal axis'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a vertical axis; 1 mark for stating it runs from the top of the head to the feet (or through the spine/centre of the body vertically) and that the body rotates around it during spinning or twisting actions.

practice_questions.text: Describe the plane and axis of movement used when a gymnast performs a cartwheel. Include the direction of movement in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the frontal plane; 1 mark for identifying the sagittal axis; 1 mark for describing the direction of movement as side-to-side (the body tips laterally over the hands, moving away from the midline).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a discus thrower spinning in a full circle before release uses the transverse plane and longitudinal axis rather than any other plane-and-axis combination.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating the movement is a horizontal rotation/spin; 1 mark for identifying the transverse plane (which divides the body into upper and lower halves); 1 mark for identifying the longitudinal axis (which runs vertically from head to feet); 1 mark for explaining that because the thrower rotates around a vertical axis — not forwards/backwards or side-to-side — neither the sagittal nor frontal planes apply.

practice_questions.text: A sports science student is asked to analyse the movement of a figure skater performing a spin entry and a subsequent jump that involves a forward somersault rotation. Analyse how the planes and axes of movement change between the spin and the somersault, and explain how understanding these differences helps a coach improve the athlete's technique.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): clearly identifies the transverse plane and longitudinal axis for the spin, with explanation that the body rotates horizontally around a vertical axis; clearly identifies the sagittal plane and transverse axis for the forward somersault, with explanation that the body rotates forward/backward around a side-to-side axis; analyses what changes between the two movements (from vertical to horizontal rotation, from longitudinal to transverse axis); links both to how coaching cues could reinforce these axes (e.g. a coach teaching the spin would cue the athlete to keep their longitudinal axis straight and centred; for the somersault they would cue tucking to increase rotation speed around the transverse axis). Sustained sporting application throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): correctly identifies both plane-axis pairs; some explanation of direction of rotation; limited or inconsistent application to coaching.

Developing (2 marks): one plane-axis pair correctly identified; basic description of direction of movement; little or no coaching application.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant term used (plane or axis) with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: A trampoline club coach argues that teaching athletes to understand planes and axes improves technical performance more than simply repeating skills. Evaluate this claim, considering both the benefits of applying planes-and-axes analysis to trampoline coaching and the limitations of this approach for beginner and intermediate performers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): evaluates benefits of planes-and-axes knowledge for coaching (e.g. understanding the sagittal plane and transverse axis helps a coach identify why a performer's somersault is losing height — they are not tucking to accelerate rotation around the transverse axis; understanding the longitudinal axis helps diagnose twisting technique); evaluates benefits for the athlete (mental model of movement helps self-correct; links plane-and-axis to joint actions covered in anatomy, deepening overall understanding of performance); evaluates limitations (beginners may lack the cognitive capacity to apply abstract spatial concepts during actual performance; practical skill repetition may be more effective in the early stages of learning; analysis can lead to over-thinking and disrupted automatic execution); provides a balanced conclusion (analysis is most valuable in the feedback phase with intermediate to advanced performers; beginners benefit more from demonstration and repetition); consistent sporting examples from trampolining throughout.

Secure (6-7 marks): identifies several benefits and at least one limitation; applies planes-and-axes knowledge to trampolining with reasonable accuracy; some balance in the argument.

Developing (3-5 marks): identifies benefits with limited limitation analysis; partially applied to trampoline context.

Emerging (1-2 marks): one relevant point about planes/axes in sport with minimal evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the golden triangle in sport?
A) The three phases of athletic training: strength, endurance and speed
B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media
C) The three main types of sports facilities: indoor, outdoor and aquatic
D) The three tiers of sports governance: local, national and international
practice_questions.marks: B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'commercialisation' in the context of sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition indicating that sport is treated as a product/business; 1 mark for linking this to financial gain or profit, or to the involvement of sponsors, media or businesses. Example full-mark answer: 'Commercialisation is the process by which sport is treated as a commercial product, with businesses investing in it to generate profit through sponsorship, media rights and merchandise sales.'

practice_questions.text: Explain two positive impacts and two negative impacts of sponsorship on performers in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any of the following, up to 4 marks total (must cover both positives and negatives for full marks):
Positive: financial security allowing full-time training (1); access to high-quality equipment and coaching (1); increased public profile through media exposure (1).
Negative: pressure to compete while injured to meet commercial obligations (1); loss of control over personal image as a brand ambassador (1); intense media scrutiny of personal life (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level hockey club has recently attracted a regional sports retailer as a kit sponsor. Analyse the impact of this sponsorship arrangement on the club, its players and the sponsoring company.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses impacts on all three parties (club, players and sponsor) with developed points and specific examples. Considers both positive and negative implications. Uses accurate commercial vocabulary (sponsorship, branding, profile, obligations). Answers read as continuous analysis, not a list.
Secure: Covers at least two of the three parties with developed points; mostly accurate; some sporting application.
Developing: Relevant points but limited development; may address only one or two parties; minimal sporting application.
Emerging: Basic or vague points; no development; may only state that sponsorship provides money without exploring implications.

Acceptable points include: Club gains kit/equipment costs covered and may attract better players (positive); club may face pressure to display sponsor logos prominently or associate with the brand (limitation); players gain professional-quality kit and raised local profile (positive); players may feel obligated to represent the brand positively off the pitch (negative); sponsor gains brand visibility at matches and through players wearing their kit (positive); sponsor risks reputational damage if players behave badly (negative); sponsor reaches a targeted local audience of sports participants (positive).

practice_questions.text: A young county-level sprinter has been offered a significant sponsorship deal by a national sportswear company. Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of accepting this deal for both the sprinter and for athletics as a sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sides for both the sprinter and the sport of athletics. Consistent use of sporting examples. Reaches a reasoned conclusion. Uses precise vocabulary (sponsorship, commercialisation, media exposure, obligations). Balanced argument throughout.
Secure: Covers advantages and disadvantages for the sprinter; some reference to the sport of athletics; generally accurate; mostly applied to a sporting context.
Developing: Mostly one-sided or focused only on the sprinter; limited reference to athletics as a sport; some relevant points but underdeveloped.
Emerging: Basic points about money being good or bad; no sporting application; descriptive rather than evaluative.

Acceptable points:
For the sprinter (advantages): financial security enabling full-time training; access to high-quality kit at no cost; raised public profile and media opportunities; pathway to further commercial deals.
For the sprinter (disadvantages): pressure to perform when injured to protect commercial value; obligations to represent the brand in specific ways; intense media scrutiny; risk of being dropped if performance declines.
For athletics (advantages): sponsorship raises the profile of the sport; funds available to invest in facilities or grassroots development; successful sponsored athletes act as role models.
For athletics (disadvantages): commercial interests may lead to scheduling being altered for broadcast convenience; focus on elite performers may divert resources from grassroots; smaller events without commercial appeal may be marginalised.

practice_questions.text: State two types of sponsorship that a professional sports club might receive.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct types: financial sponsorship (1); clothing and equipment sponsorship (1); facility/venue sponsorship (1). Answers must be qualitatively different — two examples of money-based sponsorship would score only 1 mark.

before.exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question about commercialisation, list-style answers score poorly. Each point should follow a three-step structure: state the impact, link it to how it affects a specific group (performer, sport, audience), and give a real or plausible example. On a 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ question, you must discuss both positive and negative impacts. A common error is writing only positives or only negatives — the mark scheme rewards a balanced argument. Use a ‘For X… However Y…’ structure and anchor each side to a sporting context. For example: “Sponsorship income allows elite athletes to train full-time [positive]. However, commercial pressure can force athletes to compete while injured to meet contractual obligations [negative].”

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct definition of fitness?
A) A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
B) The ability to meet the demands of the environment
C) The absence of disease or infirmity
D) The ability to perform aerobic exercise for long periods
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: B — the ability to meet the demands of the environment.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'cardiovascular endurance'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as the ability of the heart and lungs (cardio-respiratory system) to supply oxygen; 1 mark for stating this is during sustained/prolonged exercise (to working muscles).

practice_questions.text: Describe why a rugby union forward needs both strength and cardiovascular endurance to perform effectively.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing strength as needed for scrummaging/tackling/carrying the ball through contact (max force against opposition); 1 mark for describing cardiovascular endurance as needed to sustain effort across an 80-minute match (heart and lungs supplying oxygen to working muscles); 1 mark for describing how the demands switch between high-intensity bursts (strength/power) and sustained running phases (cardiovascular endurance) in a single game.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a gymnast competing on the balance beam requires balance and flexibility as two of their most important fitness components.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining balance: the gymnast must maintain their centre of mass over a 10cm-wide beam throughout routines — without static and dynamic balance, they would fall; 1 mark for explaining flexibility: the range of movement at joints must be extreme to perform splits, walkovers and leaps to the required technical standard; 1 mark for applying balance to a named movement (e.g. holding a scale on one leg requires static balance); 1 mark for applying flexibility to a named movement (e.g. a backbend walkover demands extreme spinal and hip flexibility to complete safely).

practice_questions.text: A county-level badminton player wants to improve their game. Analyse which three components of fitness are most important for elite badminton performance and explain how developing each would improve their results.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): identifies three appropriate components (e.g. agility, reaction time, coordination, muscular endurance) with a precise definition or understanding of each; for each component, provides a specific analysis of how it influences badminton performance (e.g. agility allows rapid direction changes to reach shots in the back-court corners; reaction time determines how quickly the player responds to a smash; coordination ensures the racket meets the shuttlecock cleanly); explains how developing each would improve results with sporting specificity; sustained analytical writing rather than bullet-listing.

Secure (3-4 marks): identifies three appropriate components with generally accurate descriptions; some application to badminton; explanation of development benefits present but may lack depth.

Developing (2 marks): identifies two appropriate components; limited application to badminton; development link present for at least one.

Emerging (1 mark): names one relevant component with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: A physical education teacher claims that a person must be both healthy and fit to achieve their best sporting performance. Evaluate this claim, using examples from sport to consider whether health and fitness are equally important, and whether it is possible to perform well when one is present but the other is not.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): clearly defines both health (complete physical, mental and social well-being) and fitness (ability to meet the demands of the environment) and treats them as separate variables; evaluates the claim in favour (high-level sport demands both — a footballer with an anxiety disorder affecting sleep and concentration may find their decision-making and reaction time impaired even if their cardiovascular fitness is excellent; an injured sprinter whose physical health is compromised cannot train specifically and therefore fitness declines); evaluates against the claim (elite athletes regularly perform at very high levels while managing chronic conditions that affect their health — e.g. athletes with managed asthma or diabetes who maintain world-class fitness; a performer may experience poor mental health but still maintain physical fitness through regular training); considers the relationship between them (poor health often leads to decreased fitness through an inability to train; high fitness can coexist with some health impairment); a balanced conclusion with examples from named sports or specific contexts; consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure (6-7 marks): defines health and fitness; covers both sides of the argument with sporting examples; some balance; generally accurate.

Developing (3-5 marks): distinguishes health from fitness; one-sided argument or limited examples.

Emerging (1-2 marks): basic reference to health or fitness with minimal evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Identify one way that technology is used to help officials in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any valid example of officiating technology, such as: video review/replay systems (1); sensor-based line-call or tracking systems (1); goal-line technology (1).

practice_questions.text: State two negative impacts of technology on audiences who watch sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct negative impacts: subscription/paywalled streaming pricing out lower-income fans (1); breaks in play due to technology reviews disrupting viewing experience (1); fragmentation of audiences across multiple platforms reducing shared viewing experience (1). Two near-identical points (e.g. 'it costs money' and 'it is expensive') earn only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways technology can improve the experience of watching sport for a television audience.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying the technology; 1 mark for explaining how it improves the viewer experience. Up to 4 marks (2 ways × 2 marks each).
Example points: High-definition and multi-angle cameras allow viewers to see detail they could not see in person (identification 1; explanation 1); instant slow-motion replays allow audiences to review controversial moments and understand decisions better (identification 1; explanation 1); statistical overlays and graphics provide additional context such as player speeds, distances and tactical patterns (identification 1; explanation 1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level rugby union team has recently been given access to a GPS tracking system for training sessions. The head coach wants to use the data to reduce injuries and improve conditioning. Analyse the impact this technology might have on the players and on the coaching staff.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of impacts on both players and coaching staff. Points are developed with specific examples. Both positive and negative consequences are explored. Accurate sport-science vocabulary used throughout.
Secure: Impacts on both groups covered; mostly accurate; mostly applied to a sporting context; some development of points.
Developing: Relevant points present but limited development; may focus predominantly on one group; minimal sporting application.
Emerging: Basic observations that GPS provides data or tells coaches things; no development or application to the scenario.

Acceptable points:
For players: more precise workload management may reduce injury risk (positive); data can motivate players by showing objective progress (positive); some players may feel over-monitored or anxious about being judged on data metrics (negative); performance data could lead to unfair selection decisions if taken out of context (negative).
For coaching staff: precise training load data enables more evidence-based decisions about intensity and recovery (positive); ability to identify players at elevated injury risk before injury occurs (positive); large volumes of data require time and expertise to interpret correctly (limitation); technology cost and training to use it may be a barrier for smaller clubs (limitation).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the impact of technology on the integrity and fairness of sport, considering both its benefits and its potential to undermine what makes sport valuable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation exploring multiple dimensions of fairness and integrity. Considers performers, officials and sport as a whole. Uses specific sporting examples. Reaches a reasoned, balanced conclusion. Precise vocabulary throughout.
Secure: Addresses benefits and drawbacks of technology for fairness and/or integrity; mostly accurate; mostly applied to a sporting context; generally balanced.
Developing: Mostly one-sided or vague; relevant points present but underdeveloped; limited sporting context.
Emerging: Basic statements about technology being helpful or harmful with no development or sporting application.

Acceptable points:
For integrity/fairness (benefits): officiating technology reduces incorrect decisions that affect match outcomes; drug-testing technology makes it harder for athletes to use banned substances; performance data levels the playing field by giving coaches objective information; Paralympic broadcasting technology has changed perceptions of disability sport.
Against integrity/fairness (drawbacks): unequal access to technology creates a new form of inequality between well-funded and under-resourced teams; advanced equipment innovations may give wealthy nations a technological edge; video review systems interrupt play and can reduce spontaneity; reliance on technology may erode coaches' and athletes' intrinsic knowledge and intuition; some equipment innovations have been banned after providing unfair advantages, suggesting regulation lags behind technology.

practice_questions.text: State two ways technology has changed how sports are broadcast to audiences.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct points: high-definition/multi-camera broadcasts (1); live streaming to mobile or internet-connected devices (1); instant slow-motion replay (1); statistical graphics and overlays during broadcasts (1). Two near-identical answers earn only 1 mark.

before.exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark ‘Analyse’ question about technology in sport, a common error is describing what technology does without explaining the impact. The mark scheme rewards analysis: state the technology, describe its effect, explain who benefits or loses out, and give a sporting example. Avoid vague statements such as “technology is good for sport” — be specific: “GPS tracking allows coaches to monitor a player’s sprint distance in training, enabling workload to be adjusted to reduce injury risk.” For 9-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions, always consider technology’s impact on multiple groups (performers, officials, audiences, sponsors) and ensure your argument addresses both benefits and drawbacks. A one-sided answer leaves out half of what the question asks.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes gamesmanship?
A) Behaviour that involves physically harming an opponent to gain advantage
B) Strategies that break the formal rules of the sport to achieve a result
C) Actions that are within the rules but deliberately violate the spirit of competition
D) Behaviour that shows respect and generosity towards opponents
practice_questions.marks: C) Actions that are within the rules but deliberately violate the spirit of competition [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sportsmanship' in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition identifying fair play, respect or generosity; 1 mark for linking this to treatment of opponents, officials or the rules of the sport. Example full-mark answer: 'Sportsmanship is behaviour that shows fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents, officials and the rules of the sport, placing the spirit of competition above personal gain.'

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'etiquette' in sport and give one specific sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying etiquette as unwritten rules or informal codes of conduct (not part of the official rule book); 1 mark for explaining that etiquette involves customs or traditions expected of participants; 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. tennis player acknowledging a net cord; golfer repairing divots; cricketer applauding a departing batsman). Example full-mark answer: 'Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct expected of performers in sport (1). It consists of customs and traditions that are not part of the official rules but that participants are expected to follow to show respect for the sport (1). For example, in tennis it is expected that a player will gesture to acknowledge a lucky net cord, even though there is no rule requiring this (1).'

practice_questions.text: Explain why the contract to compete is important for maintaining fair play in sport. Use a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for defining the contract to compete as an implicit agreement to abide by the rules and spirit of the sport; 1 mark for explaining that it requires competitors to give opponents a fair chance; 1 mark for explaining what happens when the contract is broken (erosion of trust, unfair outcomes); 1 mark for a valid sporting example where the contract was upheld or broken. Example: 'The contract to compete is the implicit agreement all competitors enter when they take part in sport (1). It requires athletes to follow the rules and give opponents a fair chance to succeed (1). When it is broken — for instance, if a performer uses excessive gamesmanship to intimidate an opponent or deliberately injures a rival — the principle of fair competition is undermined and public trust in the sport is damaged (1). In cricket, the contract to compete means batsmen should not use excessive time-wasting tactics to break a bowler’s rhythm if it goes beyond legitimate play (1).'

practice_questions.text: A year-10 county football player has noticed that their team’s opponents regularly engage in gamesmanship during matches, including excessive time-wasting, feigning injury and making loud comments designed to distract players during set pieces. Analyse the impact this behaviour might have on the match, the performers involved and the wider sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis across all three areas (match, performers, wider sport). Points are developed with specific examples. The distinction between gamesmanship and cheating is maintained throughout. Uses accurate vocabulary (etiquette, sportsmanship, contract to compete, spirit of sport). Continuous analytical prose rather than a list.
Secure: Covers at least two of the three areas with developed points; mostly accurate; mostly applied to a football context.
Developing: Relevant points present but limited development; may address only one area; minimal sporting context.
Emerging: Basic observations that gamesmanship is bad or unfair; no development or sporting application.

Acceptable points:
On the match: time-wasting reduces the quality of play and the time available for genuine competition (negative); it may frustrate the opposition into making errors or receiving cautions from the referee (tactical gain for gamesmanship team).
On the performers: players on the receiving end may feel demoralised, distracted or become aggressive in response (negative); players using gamesmanship may lose focus on their own technique and game plan (risk); young performers may normalise gamesmanship as acceptable behaviour (wider harm).
On the wider sport: frequent gamesmanship erodes the spectator experience (negative); it damages sport’s reputation as a model of positive values for young people (negative); officials face greater difficulty managing the game (increased pressure on officials); if gamesmanship becomes culturally accepted, the contract to compete and the spirit of the sport are undermined (structural harm to sport).

practice_questions.text: State two examples of etiquette from different sports.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct examples from different sports (any sport is acceptable). Examples: tennis player acknowledging a net cord to their opponent (1); golfer repairing a divot or raking a bunker (1); cricketer applauding a well-played innings by an opposition batsman (1); rugby player helping an opponent to their feet after a tackle (1); footballer kicking the ball into touch when an opponent is injured (1). Two examples from the same sport earn only 1 mark if they refer to the same type of behaviour.

practice_questions.text: Identify the fitness test used to measure cardiovascular endurance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: the Multi-Stage Fitness Test (accept: bleep test or 20-metre shuttle run test).

practice_questions.text: State two limitations of using fitness tests to assess a performer's ability in their sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct limitations from: tests are not sport-specific / do not replicate movements of the activity / do not replicate competitive conditions / many are sub-maximal (therefore may be inaccurate) / motivation of participant affects results / incorrect procedures reduce validity. Two near-identical answers (e.g. 'not sport-specific' and 'doesn't replicate the sport') score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Ruler Drop Test is conducted and what the score indicates about a performer's fitness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing the set-up (partner holds the ruler vertically with the 0 cm mark level with the top of the performer's open hand; performer places thumb and finger around but not touching the ruler); 1 mark for describing the procedure (ruler is dropped without warning; performer catches it as quickly as possible); 1 mark for explaining the scoring (the distance in cm the ruler falls before being caught indicates reaction time — a shorter distance indicates a faster reaction time).

practice_questions.text: Table 1 shows fitness test results for two 16-year-old county-level athletes before and after a 10-week training block. Athlete A: Illinois Agility Test — before 15.8 s, after 14.2 s. Athlete B: Illinois Agility Test — before 16.1 s, after 15.9 s. Using the data, interpret what the results suggest about the effectiveness of training for each athlete.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for comparing Athlete A's before and after scores (improved by 1.6 seconds); 1 mark for making an inference about Athlete A (training was effective / meaningful improvement in agility); 1 mark for comparing Athlete B's before and after scores (improved by only 0.2 seconds, a marginal change); 1 mark for making a contrasting inference about Athlete B (training had little effect on agility / improvement is negligible and may be within measurement error). Note: accept any valid reference to the figures quoted from the table.

practice_questions.text: A school physical education teacher wants to set up a fitness testing programme for her Year 10 GCSE class. She plans to use the Multi-Stage Fitness Test, the Illinois Agility Test and the Sit and Reach Test. Analyse the benefits and limitations of using this selection of tests to assess the overall fitness of her students.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): identifies and explains genuine benefits for at least two of the three tests (e.g. Multi-Stage Fitness Test provides quantitative cardiovascular endurance data that can be compared to national norms, motivating students with a clear score; Illinois Agility Test is practical in a school setting with minimal equipment; Sit and Reach requires only a box and gives a quick flexibility benchmark); identifies specific limitations for at least two tests (e.g. Illinois test does not replicate sport-specific agility patterns in team games; Sit and Reach reliability is affected by hamstring warm-up and whether students fully extend; Multi-Stage Fitness Test requires motivation to reach maximum level); considers the overall coverage (three tests only cover cardiovascular endurance, agility and flexibility — components like strength, power and reaction time are not assessed); sustained analytical discussion with specific reference to the tests and their sporting relevance.

Secure (3-4 marks): identifies benefits and limitations for most tests; some analysis of what the selection does or doesn't cover; generally accurate.

Developing (2 marks): identifies one benefit and one limitation; limited analysis of coverage.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant point about a test with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A sports coach argues that fitness testing should form a central part of every athlete's training programme throughout the year, not just at the start of a season. Evaluate this claim, considering the benefits of regular fitness testing and the potential drawbacks of using it too frequently or in inappropriate contexts.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): evaluates benefits of regular testing (monitors improvement over time and allows training adjustments; motivates athletes by showing progress; identifies when fitness is declining so reversibility can be addressed; provides data to compare against national norms and set goals); evaluates drawbacks of frequent testing (time taken away from actual training; testing fatigue if done too often; results can be demotivating if improvement plateaus; many tests are not sport-specific so results do not directly translate to competitive performance); evaluates context and timing (testing most appropriate at start and end of training blocks; during competition season, maintaining performance is the priority and repeated testing may disrupt preparation); provides a balanced conclusion (regular testing has value when spaced appropriately and limitations are understood; blind reliance on test scores without contextualising them is a mistake); consistent sporting examples throughout.

Secure (6-7 marks): identifies benefits and drawbacks with sporting examples; some consideration of context or timing; generally balanced.

Developing (3-5 marks): some benefits and at least one drawback; limited sporting application.

Emerging (1-2 marks): one relevant point about fitness testing with minimal evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Identify the category of performance-enhancing drug most likely to be used by a powerlifter who wants to increase muscle mass rapidly.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: anabolic agents (1) or anabolic steroids (1).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'blood doping' in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that blood doping involves removing and re-infusing blood to increase red blood cell count; 1 mark for linking this to an improvement in oxygen-carrying capacity or endurance performance. Example full-mark answer: 'Blood doping is a prohibited method in which an athlete removes a quantity of their own blood weeks before competition, stores it, and re-infuses it just before competing in order to artificially increase red blood cell count and oxygen-carrying capacity.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the effects and side effects of using EPO as a performance-enhancing substance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that EPO increases red blood cell production; 1 mark for explaining that this increases oxygen-carrying capacity and benefits endurance performance; 1 mark for a valid side effect (blood thickening/increased viscosity; risk of heart attack or stroke; risk of blood clot/embolism). Example full-mark answer: 'EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells in the body (1). More red blood cells increase the blood’s ability to carry oxygen to working muscles, improving aerobic endurance performance (1). A dangerous side effect is that EPO thickens the blood, increasing viscosity, which can lead to blood clots, heart attack or stroke (1).'

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a performer might choose to use anabolic agents, and two reasons why this decision could have serious negative consequences for them.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 reasons for + 2 consequences): must cover both sides for full marks.
Reasons for using (up to 2 marks): increased muscle mass improving strength and power performance (1); faster recovery from training enabling greater training volume (1); increased chance of competition success leading to financial reward and recognition (1).
Negative consequences (up to 2 marks): risk of liver damage and cardiovascular disease (1); hormonal disruption, including in secondary sexual characteristics (1); risk of ban, fine and permanent reputational damage if detected (1); permanent growth plate damage in adolescent users (1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level distance runner has been told by a teammate that EPO is undetectable and that many top competitors use it anyway. Evaluate the arguments for and against the runner using EPO, and reach a conclusion about whether such arguments can be justified.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation presenting genuine arguments on both sides. Challenges the ‘level playing field’ reasoning with counter-arguments. Uses accurate physiological vocabulary (red blood cells, oxygen-carrying capacity, viscosity). Reaches a reasoned, balanced conclusion. Consistent sporting application throughout.
Secure: Covers arguments for and against EPO use; mostly accurate physiological understanding; mostly applied to an endurance sporting context; generally balanced.
Developing: Mostly one-sided or acknowledges both sides without developing either; some relevant points but underdeveloped; limited sporting application.
Emerging: Basic statements that EPO is wrong or helpful without physiological explanation; no balanced argument; descriptive rather than evaluative.

Acceptable arguments for using EPO: increased red blood cells improve oxygen delivery to muscles, directly improving endurance performance; may be perceived as levelling the field if others are doping; potential for greater competition success, fame and financial reward; if truly undetectable, perceived risk of sanction is low.
Arguments against using EPO: blood thickening significantly raises risk of heart attack, stroke and embolism — particularly dangerous during sleep when heart rate is low; the ‘level playing field’ argument is flawed because many competitors do not dope; wealthier competitors access safer protocols creating new inequalities; if detected, consequences include lengthy ban, loss of results, fines and career-ending reputational damage; the use violates the contract to compete and the ethical foundations of sport; the sport of distance running suffers credibility damage from doping scandals, reducing sponsorship and audience engagement.

practice_questions.text: Describe three side effects of blood doping for a performer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark each for any three distinct side effects, or 1 mark for identifying the mechanism and 1 mark for explaining the consequence. Acceptable side effects: thickening of blood/increased viscosity (1); risk of heart attack (1); risk of stroke/embolism/blockage of a blood vessel (1); potential infection from contaminated equipment (1); risk from the transfusion process itself (1). Example 3-mark answer: 'Blood doping causes the blood to thicken as red blood cell count increases (1). This increased viscosity slows blood flow and raises the risk of a heart attack (1). There is also a risk of embolism — a blockage of a blood vessel — which can be fatal (1).'

practice_questions.text: Identify which letter of the SPORT acronym represents the idea that fitness gains can be lost when training stops.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: R — Reversibility.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'progressive overload' as it applies to a training programme.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the training load must be increased; 1 mark for stating that this increase must be gradual (over time) so the body continues to adapt and improve (accept: the stimulus must increase because the body adapts to the current load and no longer improves without a new challenge).

practice_questions.text: Describe how the FITT principles can be applied to help a club-level tennis player improve their cardiovascular endurance during pre-season.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark each for applying any three of the four FITT variables to the scenario with specific detail. Frequency example: train 4 times a week rather than twice, as cardiovascular gains require more sessions. Intensity example: set sessions at 70-80% of maximum heart rate to work in the aerobic training zone. Time example: sessions of 45-60 minutes to ensure sustained aerobic demand. Type example: use continuous training (e.g. cycling, running on court) to develop cardiovascular endurance specifically. Each answer must include the variable name and a specific application.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a coach can use the principle of specificity when designing a training programme for a 400m track cyclist.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining specificity (training must match the demands of the sport/activity); 1 mark for explaining the specific energy system demands of 400m track cycling (high-intensity anaerobic effort over approximately 40-50 seconds, with significant lactic acid production); 1 mark for explaining how training type should reflect this (interval training or HIIT on the bike, not long-distance continuous running); 1 mark for explaining how muscle specificity applies (training the quadriceps, gluteals and hip flexors through cycling-specific movements rather than gym exercises that do not replicate the cycling action).

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level distance runner has been following the same 10km running programme for three months with no improvement in race times. Analyse how the SPORT and FITT principles could be used to redesign the programme so that it leads to further performance improvements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): identifies that the lack of improvement is explained by the principle of progressive overload — the body has adapted to the current stimulus; applies at least three FITT variables specifically (e.g. increase frequency from 3 to 5 sessions per week; increase intensity by introducing 80-85% max HR threshold runs; increase time of long runs by 10% per week); identifies specificity as supporting continued running-based sessions rather than switching to a different sport; raises reversibility to advise against abrupt rest periods; avoids tedium by introducing fartlek training alongside continuous sessions; provides a coherent analysis of how these changes would lead to further cardiovascular and muscular endurance adaptation. Sporting context maintained throughout.

Secure (3-4 marks): identifies progressive overload as the issue; applies two or more FITT variables with some specificity; some reference to sport context.

Developing (2 marks): identifies that training needs to be harder or more varied; limited use of SPORT/FITT terminology.

Emerging (1 mark): one relevant principle mentioned with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A school sports coach is designing an annual training programme for a Year 11 football squad. Evaluate how effectively the SPORT principles can be applied to team sport training compared to individual sport training, considering both the benefits and the challenges for a football coach.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): evaluates each SPORT principle with a two-sided argument. Specificity: in individual sports (e.g. marathon running) specificity is straightforward — one performer, one event; in football, specificity is harder because different positions require different fitness profiles (a goalkeeper needs different components from a midfielder), so a whole-squad programme may not be fully specific for every player. Progressive overload: easy to apply individually; harder in team training because players start from different fitness baselines — a blanket 10% increase in session intensity may overload some players while under-loading others. Reversibility: applies equally to both; coaches of both individual and team sport must plan for off-season maintenance. Tedium: team sport naturally provides variety through small-sided games, drills and positional training; individual sport coaches must work harder to introduce variety. Evaluates the overall effectiveness (SPORT principles work well in team sport but require differentiation and group management strategies that individual sport coaches do not face). Balanced argument, naming specific football examples and contrasting with individual sport examples throughout.

Secure (6-7 marks): all four SPORT principles covered with some two-sided argument; mostly applied to football with some comparison to individual sport; generally accurate.

Developing (3-5 marks): at least two SPORT principles covered; limited balance; some sporting application.

Emerging (1-2 marks): basic reference to one or two principles with minimal analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a positive effect of spectators on a sporting performance?
A) Increased risk of crowd disorder
B) Excessive pressure leading to over-arousal
C) Creation of a home advantage for the home team
D) Higher security costs for the event organiser
practice_questions.marks: C) Creation of a home advantage for the home team [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why hooliganism occurs at sporting events.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two different reasons from: rivalries between teams or fan groups; hype and media build-up; alcohol or drug use; frustration at decisions or results; gang culture; display of masculinity. Answers must be qualitatively different — 'fuelled by alcohol' and 'drug use' count as one point.

practice_questions.text: Explain how banning orders are used to combat hooliganism in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying banning orders as a legal tool (civil order issued by a court). 1 mark for explaining what they prohibit (attending specified fixtures or all football matches in the country). 1 mark for explaining how they are enforced for international fixtures (offender must surrender passport or report to a police station). 1 mark for explaining why they are effective (targets repeat offenders; removes known troublemakers; reduces incidents at high-risk matches).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the effectiveness of alcohol restrictions as a strategy for reducing hooliganism at football matches.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): identifies the strategy clearly (alcohol cannot be consumed in view of the pitch; some matches enforce total bans); analyses how it reduces hooliganism (alcohol is linked to disinhibition, reducing rational decision-making; restricting it lowers the likelihood of impulsive aggressive behaviour); acknowledges a significant limitation (pre-loading before arrival is not prevented; restriction at the ground does not control consumption during travel); reaches a developed analytical conclusion — for example, alcohol restrictions are effective within the stadium but have limited impact on disorder in surrounding streets. Uses sporting context throughout.
Secure (3–4 marks): describes the strategy and gives at least one developed analysis point with a partial limitation.
Developing (2 marks): identifies the strategy with a simple reason why it helps, but limited development or no limitation.
Emerging (1 mark): basic identification of alcohol restrictions with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level rugby player has noticed that her performance drops noticeably when playing away fixtures in front of large, hostile crowds. Evaluate the extent to which spectators have a negative rather than positive impact on a performer's experience of sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): presents a balanced evaluation of both positive and negative spectator impacts; applies points consistently to a sporting context; covers at least three negative impacts (over-arousal, hostile atmosphere, deterrence of young participants, safety risks) and at least two positive impacts (atmosphere, home advantage, inspiration, financial support); reaches a clear justified conclusion about which outweighs the other, with a reasoned basis.
Secure (5–7 marks): covers both sides, mostly applied to sport; at least two negative and one positive point; some development beyond a list.
Developing (3–4 marks): relevant points on both sides but limited development; sporting context present but not always linked to the analysis.
Emerging (1–2 marks): basic points, mainly descriptive; one-sided or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A table shows annual football-related arrest figures at English grounds over five years: Year 1: 3,200; Year 2: 2,950; Year 3: 2,700; Year 4: 2,480; Year 5: 2,310. Calculate the overall change in arrests between Year 1 and Year 5, and explain what this tells us about the effectiveness of anti-hooliganism strategies.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: 3,200 minus 2,310 = 890 arrests. 1 mark for quoting both figures and stating the unit (arrests). 1 mark for a valid inference: arrests fell by 890 over five years, suggesting anti-hooliganism strategies (such as banning orders, all-seater stadia or increased security) have been increasingly effective at reducing violent spectator behaviour.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes HIIT?
A) Sustained exercise at a constant pace for at least 20 minutes
B) Short bursts of near-maximal effort alternated with brief rest periods
C) Moving around a series of exercise stations with different fitness aims
D) Stretching a muscle and holding the position for up to 30 seconds
practice_questions.marks: B) Short bursts of near-maximal effort alternated with brief rest periods [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of circuit training compared to continuous training.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of two distinct advantages, for example:
- It can target multiple components of fitness in one session (1)
- It can be adapted by changing stations, rest periods or resistance (1)
- It can replicate movements specific to a sport (1)
- It provides variety, reducing tedium (1)
Note: responses must be qualitatively different to earn both marks. 'It improves fitness' and 'it makes you fitter' count as the same point.

practice_questions.text: Describe how plyometric training develops muscular power.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- The muscle undergoes a rapid eccentric (lengthening) contraction first (1)
- Elastic energy is stored in the muscle and tendon during this phase (1)
- This is immediately followed by a powerful concentric (shortening) contraction (1)
- The rapid transition between phases (the stretch-shortening cycle) produces a greater power output than a concentric contraction alone (1)
Any three of the above points, clearly described. Credit 'eccentric then concentric' and 'stretch-shortening cycle' as trigger phrases.

practice_questions.text: Explain why fartlek training is more appropriate for a football player than continuous training.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
- Fartlek varies speed and intensity throughout the session, including bursts of high-intensity effort (1)
- This mirrors the intermittent demands of football, where players alternate between jogging, sprinting and walking (1)
- Continuous training maintains a steady pace and develops aerobic endurance only (1)
- Football requires both aerobic and anaerobic capacity, and fartlek training stresses both energy systems (1)
Full credit requires both an explanation of what fartlek does AND why this is more appropriate for football than continuous training.

practice_questions.text:
A 17-year-old club-level long jumper wants to increase her explosive leg power over a 12-week training block.

Evaluate the use of plyometric training and weight training as methods she could use to achieve this goal.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8-9 marks): A balanced evaluation of both methods. Identifies advantages and disadvantages of each, consistently applies them to a long jumper's specific needs (take-off power, sprint speed, injury risk), and reaches a justified conclusion about which method or combination is most appropriate. Uses accurate terminology throughout (eccentric/concentric, one rep max, stretch-shortening cycle, sets/reps).

Secure (5-7 marks): Discusses both methods with some application to the long jump. Advantages and disadvantages present for at least one method. Some sporting application but may be inconsistent. Generally accurate terminology.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points about one or both methods but limited development. May only list advantages without considering limitations, or may apply the points to sport only superficially.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic identification of one method's feature. Little or no application to a specific sporting context. Descriptive rather than evaluative.

practice_questions.text: A sprint coach is designing an interval training session for a 100 m sprinter. Explain how the work:rest ratio should be set to ensure the anaerobic energy system is targeted, and why this is important for the sprinter's performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
- The work period should be short and at maximal intensity (above 80% max HR / all-out sprint) (1)
- The rest period should be longer than the work period to allow ATP-PCr and anaerobic stores to partially recover (1)
- For example, a 10-second maximal sprint followed by 50–60 seconds of rest would target the ATP-PCr (anaerobic) system (1)
- This is important because a 100 m sprint is entirely anaerobic — the race lasts under 12 seconds and the intensity is too high for aerobic respiration to meet the energy demand (1)

practice_questions.text: Identify one mental health benefit of regular participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: reduces stress or tension; release of serotonin/endorphins (feel-good hormones); helps control emotions; reduces anxiety; improves mood. Accept precise physiological answers (serotonin release) or descriptive answers (reduces stress).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'social health'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition: the ability to form relationships with others / meet social needs. 1 mark for development: includes the ability to cooperate with others, belong to a community and contribute to group goals; or gives a sporting example (e.g. playing in a team sport provides social contact and a sense of belonging).

practice_questions.text: Describe three ways in which participating in team sport can improve a young person's social wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for three distinct points from: provides opportunities to socialise and make friends; develops cooperation skills (working with others towards a shared goal); develops teamwork (collective effort, shared responsibility); reduces loneliness / combats isolation; connects individuals to a community network; helps develop communication and trust.

practice_questions.text: Explain how regular exercise can improve a person's mental health, referring to at least one biological mechanism.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a benefit (reduces stress / anxiety / improves mood). 1 mark for the biological mechanism (exercise triggers release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of calm and happiness). 1 mark for a second mechanism or further development (endorphins also released, producing feelings of euphoria; or regular exercise lowers baseline cortisol levels over time). 1 mark for sporting application (a swimmer who trains regularly may find their anxiety levels reduced on school days as a result of consistent serotonin release).

practice_questions.text: A table shows the self-reported wellbeing scores (out of 10) of 40 students before and after a 6-week exercise programme: Physical wellbeing — before 5.2, after 7.1; Mental wellbeing — before 4.8, after 6.9; Social wellbeing — before 5.5, after 7.4. Using the data, calculate the mean improvement across all three dimensions of wellbeing, and explain what this suggests about the value of the programme.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: improvements are 1.9 (physical), 2.1 (mental), 1.9 (social); mean = (1.9 + 2.1 + 1.9) ÷ 3 = 5.9 ÷ 3 = 1.97 (accept 1.96 to 2.0). 1 mark for showing working and stating the unit (points on the wellbeing scale). 1 mark for a valid inference: the mean improvement of approximately 2 points across all three wellbeing dimensions suggests the programme produced balanced benefits, indicating that physical activity supports physical, mental and social health simultaneously.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how participation in physical activity can improve physical, mental and social wellbeing. Refer to specific mechanisms in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): analyses all three wellbeing dimensions with at least one specific mechanism per dimension; applies each point to a sporting example; links mechanisms to outcomes (e.g. exercise raises serotonin, which reduces anxiety, which improves daily functioning); reaches a developed analytical conclusion about the interconnected nature of the three dimensions.
Secure (3–4 marks): covers at least two dimensions with some development; sporting context mostly present; mechanisms mentioned but not fully explained.
Developing (2 marks): identifies benefits across two or more dimensions but mainly descriptive; limited sporting application.
Emerging (1 mark): one dimension only or very basic points with no sporting context.

practice_questions.text: Identify the formula used to calculate maximum heart rate.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for: maximum heart rate = 220 minus age (or 220 - age) [1 mark]
Do not accept answers that state only '220' without the subtraction of age.

practice_questions.text: A club-level cyclist is 18 years old. Calculate her aerobic training zone. Show your working and include units.
practice_questions.marks:
Max HR = 220 - 18 = 202 bpm (working must be shown)
Aerobic zone: 60% of 202 = 121.2 bpm (accept 121 bpm) to 80% of 202 = 161.6 bpm (accept 162 bpm)
1 mark for correct calculation of maximum HR (202 bpm)
1 mark for correctly calculating both boundaries of the aerobic zone with units (bpm)
Note: if the candidate states max HR incorrectly but applies 60% and 80% consistently, award the method mark but not the accuracy mark.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows a 16-year-old rugby player's heart rate at three points during a training session.

Rest: 65 bpm | End of warm-up: 118 bpm | Peak (during sprint drills): 178 bpm

His maximum heart rate is 204 bpm. Using the data, calculate his heart rate as a percentage of his maximum heart rate during the sprint drills. State whether this places him in the aerobic or anaerobic training zone.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: 178 ÷ 204 × 100 = 87.3% (accept 87%)
1 mark for correct formula or method (peak HR ÷ max HR × 100)
1 mark for the correct percentage (87% / 87.3%), with units shown
1 mark for correctly identifying this as the anaerobic training zone (80-90% of max HR)
Note: if the candidate uses a wrong percentage threshold to identify the zone, they lose the final mark only. Accept 'above the aerobic zone threshold' as equivalent.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which altitude training improves aerobic performance when an athlete returns to sea level.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 marks per way):
Way 1: At altitude, reduced oxygen availability triggers the body to produce more red blood cells (1); this increases the volume of haemoglobin, improving the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity when the athlete competes at sea level (1)
Way 2: The increased red blood cell concentration means more oxygen can be delivered to the working muscles per beat of the heart (1); this delays fatigue and improves performance in aerobic events such as the marathon or long-distance cycling (1)
Alternative Way 2: The training effect is physiological and lasts for several weeks after returning to sea level (1); athletes therefore time altitude camps carefully to peak for a major competition (1)

practice_questions.text:
A 17-year-old county-level middle-distance runner is planning her training year. She has a major regional championship in July.

Analyse how the seasonal aspects of training should be structured across the year to ensure she peaks in July.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6 marks): Accurately describes all three phases (pre-season, competition, post-season), links each phase to specific training characteristics (volume, intensity, type), and applies each to the runner's context (e.g. pre-season starts high-volume base fitness work, competition phase shifts to race-specific interval training at or above the anaerobic threshold, post-season allows physiological recovery). Uses appropriate terminology throughout (reversibility, progressive overload, training zones, peaking).

Secure (4-5 marks): Identifies two or three phases with accurate descriptions. Training characteristics mostly correct. Application to a runner present but may lack depth for one phase.

Developing (2-3 marks): Names the phases but description of training characteristics is limited or partially inaccurate. Limited application to the runner's specific event.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one phase or makes a basic true statement about seasonal training. No development or sporting application.

practice_questions.text: Explain three factors an athlete should consider to prevent injury during a weight training session.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of three distinct, developed factors, for example:
- Complete a thorough warm-up to increase muscle temperature and pliability, reducing the risk of strains (1)
- Use correct lifting technique throughout (e.g. neutral spine in deadlifts, knees tracking toes in squats) to prevent acute and overuse injuries (1)
- Select an appropriate weight that does not cause failure of technique, avoiding over-training (1)
- Use a spotter when performing heavy compound lifts such as the bench press (1)
- Wear appropriate footwear to provide joint support and stability (1)
- Maintain hydration to prevent blood thickening and maintain muscle function (1)
Any three distinct points, each explained with a reason for how it prevents injury.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the purpose of a pulse raiser in a warm-up?
A) To stretch the major muscle groups and improve flexibility
B) To gradually raise heart rate, blood flow and body temperature before exercise
C) To rehearse sport-specific movements at match intensity
D) To focus the mind and reduce competitive anxiety
practice_questions.marks: B) To gradually raise heart rate, blood flow and body temperature before exercise [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two physiological benefits of completing a warm-up before exercise.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of two distinct physiological benefits, for example:
- Increased body temperature makes muscles more pliable, reducing the risk of strains (1)
- Increased range of movement at joints as synovial fluid becomes less viscous (1)
- Increased heart rate and cardiac output gradually prepare the cardiovascular system (1)
- Increased oxygen delivery to working muscles (1)
- Nerve impulse transmission speeds up, improving reaction time and muscle contraction speed (1)
Note: two answers must be physiologically distinct to earn both marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how cooling down helps the body recover from intense exercise. Include reference to lactic acid in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- Gradual reduction in intensity maintains elevated heart rate and blood flow to the muscles (1)
- Sustained blood flow transports lactic acid away from the muscles to the liver and kidneys for processing and removal (1)
- This reduces the acidity in the muscles and helps prevent or minimise DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) (1)
- Static stretching during the cool-down helps maintain muscle flexibility and reduce post-exercise tightness (1)
Any three of the above, with lactic acid specifically referenced for at least one mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain why skill familiarisation is included in a warm-up, and how it differs from the pulse raiser.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
- Skill familiarisation involves sport-specific drills and movements at moderate intensity (1)
- It prepares the neuromuscular system by rehearsing the precise movement patterns required in the activity (1)
- It builds confidence and bridges the gap between general preparation and full competition demands (1)
- The pulse raiser is non-specific (general aerobic activity such as jogging) and focuses on raising heart rate and body temperature rather than rehearsing skills (1)
Full marks require both an explanation of skill familiarisation's purpose AND a clear distinction from the pulse raiser.

practice_questions.text:
A Year-12 county-level netball team has 20 minutes before a regional quarter-final. Their coach is planning the warm-up.

Analyse the importance of each component of an effective warm-up for the netball players before this match.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6 marks): All four components identified and each clearly linked to a physiological or psychological benefit specific to netball. For example: pulse raiser raises body temperature and increases blood flow to muscles needed for explosive movement and change of direction; stretching increases joint range of movement particularly at the hip and shoulder, needed for shooting and defensive reaching; skill familiarisation with passing drills and footwork patterns activates the neuromuscular pathways specific to netball decision-making; mental preparation reduces pre-match anxiety and sharpens decision-making under pressure. Uses accurate physiological terminology throughout.

Secure (4-5 marks): Three or four components described with correct benefits. At least two benefits applied to netball specifically. Generally accurate terminology.

Developing (2-3 marks): Two components identified and described. Limited sporting application. One or more physiological effects correctly stated.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one component or states one general benefit of warming up without development or application.

practice_questions.text: State two benefits of including static stretching in a cool-down.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of two distinct benefits:
- Helps maintain or improve flexibility over time as muscles are warm and pliable after exercise (1)
- Reduces post-exercise muscle stiffness and tightness (1)
- Helps reduce the severity of DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness) (1)
- Allows muscle fibres to return towards their resting length after sustained contraction (1)

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an endomorph body type?
A) Muscular with wide shoulders, narrow waist and low body fat
B) Lean with long limbs, narrow hips and low muscle mass
C) Pear-shaped with wide hips, high body fat and relatively narrow shoulders
D) Athletic with a high strength-to-weight ratio and well-defined musculature
practice_questions.marks: C) Pear-shaped with wide hips, high body fat and relatively narrow shoulders [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'sedentary lifestyle'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition: a way of living characterised by very little physical activity / spending most of the day sitting or inactive. 1 mark for development: identifies the health risks this creates (e.g. increased risk of obesity, heart disease and diabetes) or gives a specific example of sedentary behaviour (e.g. sitting at a screen for several hours a day without structured exercise).

practice_questions.text: Describe three consequences of living a sedentary lifestyle.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for three distinct consequences from: weight gain/obesity; heart disease; hypertension (high blood pressure); diabetes (type 2); poor sleep; poor self-esteem; lethargy. Answers that name very similar consequences (e.g. 'heart disease' and 'heart attacks') count as one consequence. Accept physical, mental or social consequences.

practice_questions.text: Explain why obesity limits a performer's ability to participate effectively in team sports.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a performance component limited by obesity (cardiovascular endurance/agility/flexibility/speed). 1 mark for explaining why obesity limits that component (e.g. excess body fat increases the mass the muscles must move, reducing speed; or excess fat restricts range of movement at joints, reducing flexibility and agility). 1 mark for a second performance component and explanation. 1 mark for a sporting application (e.g. in football, an obese player would struggle to maintain the cardiovascular endurance needed for 90 minutes of play and would be slower when accelerating into space).

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old aspiring marathon runner has been assessed by her coach. She is described as having a lean, slender build, long legs, narrow hips and shoulders, and very low body fat. Analyse the extent to which her somatotype is suited to marathon running and whether it presents any disadvantages.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): correctly identifies the somatotype as ectomorphic; analyses the advantages for marathon running in detail (low body fat reduces mass to be carried, long limbs provide efficient stride length, low mass reduces oxygen demand per kilometre); analyses at least one disadvantage with development (low muscle mass may limit hill climbing power; susceptibility to cold weather in long-distance outdoor racing; increased injury risk from impact forces on slender limbs); reaches a developed analytical conclusion weighing advantages against disadvantages in this specific sport.
Secure (3–4 marks): identifies somatotype, gives at least two advantages with some development and one disadvantage; sporting context mostly present.
Developing (2 marks): identifies somatotype and gives one or two simple points but limited analysis or no disadvantage considered.
Emerging (1 mark): names the somatotype with little or no justification.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether the consequences of a sedentary lifestyle are more serious for physical health than for mental and social health.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): presents a balanced evaluation across all three health dimensions; argues why physical consequences (obesity, heart disease, hypertension, diabetes) may be considered most serious (life-limiting, potentially fatal); argues why mental consequences (depression, poor self-esteem, lethargy creating a self-perpetuating cycle) may be equally or more serious (harder to identify and treat, reinforce the sedentary lifestyle); argues why social consequences (isolation, inability to leave home) compound both; reaches a clear, justified conclusion about which dimension presents the greatest long-term risk, with evidence from the lesson.
Secure (5–7 marks): covers all three dimensions; makes a case for at least one side with development; partial counter-argument; some sporting or health context.
Developing (3–4 marks): covers physical and one other dimension; some development but limited evaluation; conclusion present but not fully justified.
Emerging (1–2 marks): basic list of consequences; one-dimensional; no evaluation of relative severity.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of data produced when a coach times a swimmer's 50 m length and records it in seconds.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for: quantitative data [1 mark]
Do not accept 'numerical' alone without the term 'quantitative', unless the explanation makes clear it is measurable/countable data.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the number of students participating in four sports at Redmoor Academy during one lunchtime session.

Netball: 22 students | Football: 38 students | Badminton: 14 students | Athletics: 16 students

Calculate the mean number of students participating across the four sports.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: (22 + 38 + 14 + 16) = 90 ÷ 4 = 22.5 students
1 mark for correct addition and division method shown (90 ÷ 4)
1 mark for the correct answer: 22.5 students (accept 22-23 if rounded, but deduct final mark if no working shown)
Note: units (students) should be included. Award 1 mark only if no working is shown but the answer is correct.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows three Year-10 students' sit-and-reach test scores (cm) at the start and end of a 10-week flexibility training programme.

Student A: Start 18 cm, End 24 cm
Student B: Start 14 cm, End 17 cm
Student C: Start 21 cm, End 28 cm

Calculate Student C's percentage improvement in flexibility. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: change = 28 - 21 = 7 cm; percentage change = 7 ÷ 21 × 100 = 33.3%
1 mark for correctly identifying the change (28 - 21 = 7 cm)
1 mark for applying the correct percentage change formula (7 ÷ 21 × 100)
1 mark for the correct answer with units: 33.3% (accept 33% or 33.3%)
Always show the formula and substitution. Correct answer without working scores 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text:
Bar Chart 1 shows weekly participation rates (% of registered members) in three sports at a local sports centre across a 4-week period.

Week 1: swimming 45%, fitness suite 62%, team sports 28%
Week 2: swimming 48%, fitness suite 65%, team sports 31%
Week 3: swimming 47%, fitness suite 70%, team sports 29%
Week 4: swimming 44%, fitness suite 74%, team sports 30%

Interpret what the data shows about participation trends at this sports centre.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Responses must compare figures (not just describe one figure), quote a specific value, and explain the implication:
- Fitness suite participation shows a consistent upward trend from 62% in week 1 to 74% in week 4, a rise of 12 percentage points, suggesting growing engagement with gym-based exercise (1 mark for comparison + implication)
- Swimming participation remained relatively stable (range 44-48%), suggesting a steady core user group with little growth or decline (1)
- Team sports participation was consistently the lowest across all four weeks (range 28-31%), which may indicate barriers to participation in team activities compared to individual exercise options (1)
- The gap between fitness suite and team sports participation widened from 34 percentage points in week 1 to 44 in week 4, suggesting individual exercise formats are growing in popularity relative to team sports (1)
Award marks for any four distinct, developed interpretations with specific data references.
