practice_questions.text:
A sports scientist is studying the effects of a 12-week cardiovascular training programme on three Year-11 students. She wants to collect both quantitative and qualitative data.

Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of using interviews compared to fitness tests to collect data for this study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (6 marks): Clearly identifies both methods, accurately explains the type of data each produces (qualitative vs quantitative), and develops both advantages and disadvantages of each in the context of this specific study. For example: fitness tests produce quantitative data (e.g. multi-stage fitness test score) that can be compared to national norms and tracked statistically across 12 weeks, providing objective evidence of improvement; however, they may not reflect how the students feel about their progress or engagement, which matters for long-term adherence. Interviews produce qualitative data (rich descriptions of experience and motivation), but results are harder to compare between students and may be influenced by social desirability (students say what the researcher wants to hear). Reaches a justified conclusion about when each is most appropriate.

Secure (4-5 marks): Identifies both methods with correct data types. Advantages and disadvantages present for at least one method. Some application to the study. Generally accurate.

Developing (2-3 marks): Describes one method accurately, or mentions both with limited development. Limited application to the study.

Emerging (1 mark): Names a method or correctly identifies quantitative or qualitative without development.

practice_questions.text:
A coach records the following resting heart rate data for an athlete across a 6-week training programme: Week 1: 72 bpm, Week 2: 70 bpm, Week 3: 69 bpm, Week 4: 67 bpm, Week 5: 65 bpm, Week 6: 63 bpm.

Calculate the range of the data set and explain what it suggests about the athlete's adaptation to training.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: range = 72 - 63 = 9 bpm
1 mark for correct calculation: highest (72) - lowest (63) = 9 bpm (unit required)
1 mark for identifying the trend: resting heart rate decreased consistently over 6 weeks
1 mark for explaining the adaptation: this is bradycardia, the long-term effect of cardiovascular training, where the heart becomes stronger and pumps more blood per beat (increased stroke volume), so it needs to beat less often at rest

practice_questions.text: Identify the macronutrient that the body uses as its main and preferred energy source for all types of exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: carbohydrate (accept carbs / glucose / glycogen — the macronutrient name is the target).

practice_questions.text: A sports nutritionist tells a 16-year-old female athlete that her daily diet provides 2,200 Kcal. Calculate the minimum and maximum amount of energy (in Kcal) that should come from carbohydrate in her balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: Formula: Kcal from carbohydrate = total Kcal × percentage. Minimum: 2,200 × 0.55 = 1,210 Kcal (1 mark). Maximum: 2,200 × 0.60 = 1,320 Kcal (1 mark). Both values required for full marks; unit (Kcal) must be stated or implied by context.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the daily food intake of two junior rugby players during a pre-season training week.

Player | Total daily Kcal | % from carbohydrate | % from protein | % from fat
Jamie  | 3,100 Kcal       | 50%                 | 20%            | 30%
Tyler  | 3,100 Kcal       | 58%                 | 17%            | 25%

Using the data, calculate the number of Kcal that Tyler obtains from carbohydrate each day, and state whether his carbohydrate intake falls within the recommended range for a balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: Working: 3,100 × 0.58 = 1,798 Kcal from carbohydrate (1 mark for correct working). Final answer: 1,798 Kcal (1 mark). Balanced diet range is 55–60%, so 58% falls within the recommended range (1 mark for correct judgement with reference to the 55–60% figure). Unit (Kcal) must be present.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows the resting and exercising heart rates of two athletes before and after a 90-minute training session in hot conditions. Athlete A drank water throughout; Athlete B drank nothing.

Athlete | Heart rate before session (bpm) | Heart rate at 75 min (bpm)
A       | 68                              | 142
B       | 70                              | 167

Interpret what the data shows about the effect of dehydration on Athlete B's heart rate, and explain why this change occurred.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Athlete B's heart rate is higher than Athlete A's at 75 minutes (167 bpm vs 142 bpm — a difference of 25 bpm). 1 mark for a comparison that quotes both figures. 1 mark for linking the higher heart rate to dehydration causing increased blood viscosity (thicker blood). 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: the heart must beat faster/work harder to maintain blood flow to muscles when blood is thicker. Quoting figures without making a comparison earns 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: A club-level triathlete has been advised by her coach to increase her protein intake during a 10-week strength-building phase. Analyse how an appropriate increase in protein, alongside sufficient carbohydrate, would support her training adaptations over this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Sustained analysis linking protein's role in muscle repair and hypertrophy to strength adaptations; explains that protein alone is insufficient without carbohydrate to fuel training sessions (carbohydrate = preferred energy source, all intensities); applies correctly to the triathlete context (heavy training, strength-building); may reference recovery between sessions; accurate use of terms (hypertrophy, glycogen, muscle fibre repair). Secure (3–4 marks): Accurate points about protein's role in repair/growth and carbohydrate as fuel; at least one point linked to the athlete's context; some development of each point. Developing (2 marks): Correct function of protein stated (growth and repair); carbohydrate mentioned; limited development or application to sport. Emerging (1 mark): One basic accurate point about protein or carbohydrate in isolation, with little or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 PE class has been asked whether the government should make sports drinks mandatory for school athletes during competition. Evaluate whether sports drinks are necessary to maintain hydration and performance during school-level sport, considering the consequences of dehydration.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8–9 marks): Balanced, sustained evaluation with both sides argued; consequences of dehydration cited accurately (increased blood viscosity, raised heart rate, slowed reactions, muscle cramps, impaired decision-making); counter-argument addresses the reality that most school-level sport is short-duration and water is sufficient; may distinguish between low-intensity school sport and high-intensity endurance events; correct use of terminology throughout; sporting examples used to anchor both sides. Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides present; dehydration consequences mostly accurate; sporting application present; some terminology. Developing (3–4 marks): One side argued well; dehydration mentioned but effects may be listed without development; limited balance. Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about hydration being important with little or no balance or application.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of data that is collected through interviews and deals with descriptions and opinions.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: qualitative data (accept qualitative).

practice_questions.text: A local swimming club recorded 120 junior members in 2022. By 2025, membership had grown to 156 members. Calculate the percentage change in junior membership between 2022 and 2025.
practice_questions.marks: Working: (156 minus 120) divided by 120 multiplied by 100 = 36 divided by 120 multiplied by 100 = 30% (1 mark for correct working or method). Final answer: 30% (1 mark). Unit (%) must be present. Accept 30 if % is clearly implied.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the mean resting heart rate (bpm) of 20 students in a Year-11 PE class, measured at the start and end of a 6-week cardiovascular training programme.

Measurement point | Mean resting HR (bpm) | Highest value | Lowest value
Week 1 (start)    | 72                    | 84            | 61
Week 6 (end)      | 65                    | 78            | 54

Using the data, calculate the change in mean resting heart rate and state what this suggests about the class's cardiovascular fitness.
practice_questions.marks: Working: 72 minus 65 = 7 bpm decrease (1 mark for working shown). Correct figure: 7 bpm (1 mark). Correct unit: bpm (1 mark — note this is already implied by the table but must be stated in the answer). The decrease in mean resting heart rate suggests that cardiovascular fitness improved over the 6-week programme — accept equivalent statement linking lower resting HR to improved cardiac efficiency. Do not accept 'heart rate improved' without direction.

practice_questions.text:
Figure 1 shows the weekly participation in sport and physical activity by gender and age group at a local leisure centre.

Age group | Male participation (%) | Female participation (%)
11–16     | 62                     | 41
17–24     | 55                     | 35
25–34     | 48                     | 38
35+       | 44                     | 29

Interpret what the data shows about engagement patterns in sport and physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that male participation is higher than female participation across all age groups (with at least one pair of figures quoted, e.g. 11–16: 62% vs 41%). 1 mark for a calculated difference or comparison between two groups (e.g. the largest gender gap is in the 11–16 group, where males are 21 percentage points higher). 1 mark for observing a trend in one or both genders (e.g. participation declines with age for both genders — males from 62% to 44%). 1 mark for a sporting/wellbeing explanation (e.g. this suggests that strategies to increase female participation and to retain older adults are needed; declining rates with age may reflect increased family commitments, reduced leisure time or lack of accessible provision). Answers that simply list figures without comparison earn 1 mark maximum.

practice_questions.text: A health researcher presents data to a school showing that 34% of Year-9 students at the school have low physical activity levels, compared to a national figure of 22%. Analyse how data of this kind can be used to address engagement patterns in sport and physical activity at that school.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Sustained analysis of how the data identifies a specific problem (school rate significantly exceeds national average — a 12-percentage-point difference); analysis of how this data could inform targeted interventions (e.g. timetable changes, extra-curricular opportunities, socio-economic support, removing cost barriers); may reference the factors that affect engagement patterns (accessibility, socio-economic factors, role models, family commitments); applies accurately to the school context throughout; uses data literacy terminology. Secure (3–4 marks): Accurate points about using data to identify the problem and suggest at least one strategy; sporting context present; some development. Developing (2 marks): Identifies that the school's rate is higher than the national average; mentions that something should be done; limited development. Emerging (1 mark): A basic point about data showing participation is low, with no analysis.

practice_questions.text: A national sports governing body publishes a report showing that female participation in competitive team sport has risen by 18% over five years, while male participation has remained flat. Evaluate how useful data on participation trends is for improving engagement patterns in sport and physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8–9 marks): Balanced evaluation arguing both the uses and limitations of participation data; strengths argued (identifies disparities, allows targeted funding and policy, tracks progress, supports case for role models and media coverage); limitations argued (quantitative data cannot explain why patterns exist — interviews/qualitative needed; averages may mask regional or socio-economic variation; self-reporting bias in surveys; data may be out of date); both sides applied to a named sporting context; consistent use of terminology (engagement patterns, quantitative, qualitative, socio-economic); justified conclusion. Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides present; mostly accurate; some sporting application; some terminology. Developing (3–4 marks): One side argued well; limited or no engagement with limitations of data; partial balance. Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about data being useful, with no evaluation of its limitations.
